Personalized coaching via coachable health age and counterfactual wearable trajectories

Simon A. Abstract

Personalized health coaching requires moving beyond retrospective wearable summaries toward quantitative, actionable behavioral prescriptions. Here, we introduce Coachable Health Age (CHA), an interpretable health-age metric constructed from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals passively captured by consumer wearables. Across the WEAR-ME (N=2,780N=2{,}780), All of Us (N=22,748N=22{,}748), and longitudinal Fitbit (N=1,464N=1{,}464) cohorts, CHA aligns with established cardiometabolic health and risk scores and it improves prognostic discrimination for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and body mass index. To enable prospective behavioral optimization, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned wearable world model pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of longitudinal sensor data from approximately 100,000 participants. SensorWM forecasts multi-week physiological trajectories conditioned on behavioral actions (R2R^{2} = 0.664), outperforming a general-purpose time-series foundation model while preserving clinically relevant information for downstream prediction tasks, including diabetes and hypertension. Finally, we integrate CHA and SensorWM into an agentic counterfactual coaching system to synthesize personalized 12-week coaching plans. In blinded paired reviews, certified lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over plans grounded in wearable history alone for overall quality (71.4%, P<0.001P<0.001) and anticipated adherence (71.0%, P<0.001P<0.001). Board-certified clinicians endorsed safe exercise-intensity limits in 99.2% of ratings of counterfactual-grounded plans and 97.6% of ratings of comparison plans. Automated evaluations across the full cohort also favored counterfactual-grounded plans. These findings establish a framework integrating longitudinal wearable tracking, action-conditioned physiological forecasting, and personalized coaching, supporting prospective evaluation of its effects on behavioral adherence and cardiometabolic health.

1 Main

A substantial proportion of the global burden of chronic disease, particularly cardiometabolic disease, is attributable to modifiable behaviors such as physical inactivity, poor sleep, and unhealthy diet, and is therefore preventable Lloyd-Jones et al. (2022); Vaduganathan et al. (2022). Translating this preventive potential into sustained behavior change requires measures of health that are personalized, intuitive, and responsive to changes in daily behavior. Although chronological age is among the strongest predictors of mortality and chronic disease, it fails to capture the substantial heterogeneity in physiological function among individuals of the same age. Biological or health age measures have therefore been developed from molecular, clinical and wearable-derived features to quantify deviations from expected age-related physiology Klemera and Ďoubal (2006); Levine et al. (2018); Miller et al. (2025). By expressing multidimensional physiological information on a familiar age scale, these measures can make health status more interpretable and personally salient Spiegelhalter (2016). Related constructs such as “heart age” and “fitness age” have been used to communicate risk in accessible termsBonner et al. (2021) and in some trials such framing has improved risk perception and health behaviors, including smoking cessation Parkes et al. (2008), although effects have been inconsistent Bonner et al. (2021); Bakhit et al. (2024). Tracked longitudinally, health age could additionally serve as a feedback signal linking daily behaviors to longer-term changes in physiological state.

Most existing approaches derive health age by training machine-learning models to predict chronological age from multiple clinical biomarkers, or continuous wearable data Horvath (2013); Pyrkov et al. (2018); Miller et al. (2025), with a predicted age below chronological age, a negative age delta, interpreted as evidence of biological youthfulness or more favorable functional health. Second generation clocks trained on mortality or phenotypic outcomes improve risk predictions Levine et al. (2018); McCrory et al. (2021), but like age trained models, they are optimized to capture risk rather than modifiability. Chronological age prediction and health coaching are not completely aligned objectives. A model optimized to predict chronological age or mortality risk may rely on physiological characteristics that are strongly age-associated but fixed, difficult to modify, or only weakly informative about behaviors an individual can act upon. They are also typically opaque; post hoc attribution methods can indicate which inputs influenced an estimate, but not how that estimate would change if a person altered their behaviorGhassemi et al. (2021). A health-age measure intended for coaching should therefore be built from interpretable, repeatedly measurable characteristics that can serve as practical targets for behavioral feedback Michie et al. (2009); Michie et al. (2013); Bandura (2004).

A coachable health-age measure describes an individual’s current state. Prospective coaching additionally requires understanding how that state may evolve by comparing health trajectories under alternative behavioral scenarios Hood and Flores (2012). The density and continuity of consumer-wearable signals make them well suited to this task. Recurrent and transformer models have been used to model physiological states and incident risk from longitudinal health records and wearable data Rajkomar et al. (2018); Miller et al. (2025). This work has culminated in large-scale wearable “foundation models” trained using self-supervised objectives across thousands to millions of participants, which learn general-purpose physiological representations Abbaspourazad et al. (); Narayanswamy et al. (2026); Lee et al. (2026b); Zhou et al. (2026); Cao et al. (2026); Jing et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026) and support imputation and interpolation of sensor values over time Narayanswamy et al. (2025). In parallel, the digital-twin paradigm proposes individualized virtual replicas that simulate personal health trajectories to enable anticipatory care Katsoulakis et al. (2024); Lee et al. (2026a). These approaches are predominantly observational. They estimate the future associated with observed or persisting behavioral patterns. Related longitudinal outcome-modeling methods have considered predictions under alternative treatment sequences Lim et al. (2018); Bica et al. (2020); Melnychuk et al. (2022); Urbut et al. (2026), while action-conditioned world models provide a general computational framework for representing how predicted future states depend on specified actions Ha and Schmidhuber (2018); LeCun and others (2022). For wearable health coaching, however, the relevant actions are not primarily discrete clinical treatments, but continuously varying behaviors such as physical activity, sleep, and cardiovascular exercise. This motivates an action-conditioned wearable sensor model that can generate individualized physiological projections under feasible behavioral scenarios and summarize those projections using a common, coachable outcome.

Translating such projections into guidance that people can follow is a further challenge. Large language models (LLMs) can deliver personalized, conversational health coaching and have shown expert-level performance in interpreting wearable sleep and fitness data Merrill et al. (2026); Khasentino et al. (2025); Heydari et al. (2025). However, current LLM-based health coaches are typically grounded in retrospective summaries of an individual’s data rather than in quantitative projections of how their physiology would respond to specific behavioral changes, yielding recommendations that rely on qualitative population heuristics rather than calibrated, individualized dose-response estimatesKhasentino et al. (2025); Merrill et al. (2026). Moreover, LLMs can generate plausible but unsupported claims Thirunavukarasu et al. (2023), and despite recent benchmarks in wearable-based coaching Khasentino et al. (2025); Heydari et al. (2025), few systems have been rigorously evaluated by both lifestyle-coaching and clinical experts Bedi et al. (2025). Coupling LLM coaching with an explicit model of physiological response and an interpretable outcome measure could make recommendations both personalized and directly traceable to their projected health benefits.

Here, we introduce Coachable Health Age (CHA), an interpretable health-age measure built from physiological and behavioral signals that are passively and repeatedly measured by consumer wearables, including resting heart rate, sleep duration and physical activity, and that reflect modifiable aspects of everyday health. We embed CHA within an architecture that couples an action-conditioned wearable Sensor World Model (SensorWM) with an agentic coaching system. The world model learns predictive physiological dynamics from longitudinal wearable trajectories and generates model-implied future states conditioned on alternative patterns of daily activity, sleep, and structured exercise. The coaching agent integrates these counterfactual projections with a feasibility-constrained optimization procedure to produce personalized behavioral plans grounded in projected changes in CHA. We evaluate each component of the framework, assessing the clinical, prognostic, and longitudinal validity of CHA, the forecasting fidelity of SensorWM in driving the coaching simulation engine, the behavior of its scenario-conditioned projections, and the quality of coaching plans generated with and without simulation-derived information. In blinded evaluations, lifestyle coaches consistently preferred plans informed by CHA and SensorWM projections over plans grounded in baseline wearable data alone for overall plan quality and anticipated long-term adherence, and clinicians rated both sets of plans similarly on exercise-intensity safety and physiological accuracy.

2 Results

2.1 Study design and dataset characteristics

We designed the study as three linked analyses evaluating the core components of our end-to-end CHA and counterfactual coaching framework (Figure 1; cohort demographics and baseline wearable characteristics in Table 1). First, we constructed and evaluated CHA, an age-equivalent summary of wearable-derived physiological and behavioral health built from repeatedly measurable, modifiable signals (Figure 1a). We assessed its alignment against established cardiovascular and metabolic health and risk scores (modified Life’s Essential 8 and Metabolic Syndrome Severity) and self-reported health in the WEAR-ME cohort, and characterized its within-person longitudinal modifiability across repeated 3-month windows over two years in the longitudinal Fitbit cohort. Independent prospective clinical validation was then performed in the All of Us Research Program by relating baseline and longitudinal Δ​CHA\Delta\text{CHA} (Δ​CHA=CHA−chronological age\Delta\text{CHA}=\text{CHA}-\text{chronological age}) to incident cardiometabolic disease, specifically hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease as well as incremental prognostic discrimination beyond age, sex, and body mass index (Figure 1b).

Second, we developed SensorWM, an action-conditioned latent world model for longitudinal wearable data (Figure 1c). SensorWM was pretrained on real world longitudinal wearable trajectories from 96,957 participants (approximately 100,000), comprising 2.28 million total person-weeks of wearable data (182,797 valid 12-week windows; 42,039 person-years). The model was trained to represent physiological state in a latent space and to predict its future evolution conditional on both recent physiological trajectory and observed behavioral actions. Model fidelity was evaluated by comparing generated and observed physiological trajectories, feature-level forecasting accuracy, and preservation of clinically relevant information on downstream health prediction tasks in a held-out WEAR-ME cohort.

Third, we evaluated whether grounding an LLM coaching agent in CHA and SensorWM counterfactual projections improved personalized 12-week behavioral prescriptions (Figure 1d,e). For each eligible WEAR-ME participant, SensorWM was initialized from recent wearable history to simulate future physiological trajectories under candidate modifications in daily steps, sleep duration, and cardiorespiratory exercise. Candidate trajectories were mapped to projected changes in CHA and ranked using a feasibility-constrained optimization objective that balances projected CHA reduction against participant-specific behavioral effort and safety bounds (Figure 1d). We then compared two matched LLM coaching conditions that shared the same underlying language model, participant wearable history, and plan structure, differing only in access to simulation-derived information: (1) Counterfactual Coaching, which received the participant’s baseline CHA, projected status-quo trajectory, and feasibility-ranked counterfactual pathways, and (2) Generic Coaching, which generated recommendations from observed baseline wearable history alone. Plan quality, clinical safety, physiological plausibility, and anticipated long-term adherence were evaluated through a blinded, randomized dual-track human expert study with five certified lifestyle coaches and five board-certified clinicians across stratified WEAR-ME personas, complemented by a full-cohort automated evaluation across the WEAR-ME dataset using rubric-aligned LLM autoraters (Figure 1e). All plan generation and expert evaluations were conducted offline using retrospective participant profiles prior to prospective deployment.

2.2 Coachable Health Age Framework

To serve as both a continuous summary of everyday health and a quantitative target for prospective behavioral coaching, a health-age measure must satisfy seven core design criteria (Supplementary Table 2): it must be (1) predictable from consumer wearables via passive, high-frequency sensing; (2) explainable at the level of individual inputs; (3) flexible and extensible to additional features; (4) engageable for longitudinal user communication; (5) coachable, mapping directly to modifiable daily habits; (6) movable within individuals over coaching relevant timescales; and (7) grounded in clinical outcomes. Existing age formulations satisfy only subsets of these requirements. Chronological age provides an intuitive reference scale but cannot capture physiological heterogeneity among peers of the same age. Machine learning clocks trained to predict chronological age from wearable streams (such as foundation-model embeddings) capture age correlated sensor variation, but their training objective does not prioritize modifiable behaviors or present cardiometabolic health, and their black-box representations limit actionable attribution. Conversely, clinical biological clocks such as PhenoAge are grounded in mortality-associated blood biomarkers, but rely on invasive, episodic laboratory draws that cannot be tracked continuously by consumer wearables. Finally, directly prompting large language models (LLMs) to estimate a numerical health age from wearable summaries introduces stochastic variation across inference settings and lacks deterministic epidemiological calibration (evaluated separately in Supplementary Information A.1: LLM Health Age & Consistency).

We therefore formulated Coachable Health Age (CHA) by mapping repeatedly measurable, modifiable wearable signals, core behaviors and physiology comprising resting heart rate, daily steps, sleep duration, and weekly Active Zone Minutes (AZM)—onto an intuitive age-equivalent scale using collinearity-adjusted epidemiological hazard ratios (Figure 2a; Methods). Two architectural choices distinguish this framework. First, rather than parameterizing risk solely against late-life all-cause mortality, CHA anchors its core wearable domains to published epidemiological associations with cardiometabolic outcomes, including type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and cardiovascular disease, emphasizing risk factors that are measurable through consumer wearables and potentially responsive to behavioral modification. Second, because CHA aggregates risk additively in log-hazard space rather than through a monolithic neural network, the framework is inherently modular and expandable: optional wearable or clinical signals such as cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2​max\mathrm{VO}_{2}\max), sleep midpoint regularity, and wearable-estimated insulin resistance, or emerging sensing modalities can be seamlessly incorporated when available without retraining the underlying formulation. Together, these design characteristics motivate CHA as an interpretable, cardiometabolic grounded outcome metric (Supplementary Table 2) and reflect design considerations rather than an empirical ranking of alternative age measures.

2.3 Cardiometabolic prognosis and longitudinal modifiability of CHA

Because CHA incorporates modifiable lifestyle and physiological domains emphasized in preventive cardiometabolic disease, we first verified its alignment against established clinical health and risk scores namely modified Life’s Essential 8 (mod-LE8) and Metabolic Syndrome Severity Score (MSSS) as well as independent self-reported health status in the WEAR-ME cohort (Supplementary Figure 1). Whereas wearable models trained to predict chronological age showed weak concordance with current cardiometabolic health (mod-LE8 |r|=0.141|r|=0.141; MSSS |r|≤0.048|r|\leq 0.048) and direct LLM-based health-age estimates were poorly calibrated (|r|=0.110​–​0.214|r|=0.110\text{--}0.214), CHA preserved strong alignment with both mod-LE8 (|r|=0.512|r|=0.512) and MSSS (|r|=0.355|r|=0.355), exceeding blood-based PhenoAge (|r|=0.406|r|=0.406 and |r|=0.319|r|=0.319, respectively) and varying monotonically across self-reported health categories from excellent to poor. Thus, unlike wearable clocks, CHA directly reflects an individual’s current cardiometabolic and perceived health.

To independently validate the prognostic utility of CHA, we evaluated longitudinal incident cardiometabolic disease in the All of Us Research Program wearable cohort (N=22,748N=22{,}748, of whom N=18,423N=18{,}423 were free of all three conditions at baseline and N=4,325N=4{,}325 had pre-existing baseline disease; Figure 1b). Compared with healthy controls who remained disease-free throughout follow-up (N=17,006N=17{,}006; mean Δ​CHA=−0.43\Delta\text{CHA}=-0.43 years, 95%​ CI:[−0.47,−0.39]95\%\text{ CI}:[-0.47,-0.39]), baseline Δ​CHA\Delta\text{CHA} was higher among participants who subsequently developed incident hypertension (N=1,263N=1{,}263; −0.30-0.30 years, [−0.44,−0.15][-0.44,-0.15]), cardiovascular disease (N=589N=589; +0.23+0.23 years, [+0.01,+0.45][+0.01,+0.45]), or type 2 diabetes (N=505N=505; +0.37+0.37 years, [+0.12,+0.62][+0.12,+0.62]; Figure 1b). Over up to 36 quarters of follow-up, Kaplan–Meier analyses confirmed that baseline accelerated agers (Δ​CHA>0\Delta\text{CHA}>0, n=7,726n=7{,}726) experienced significantly lower cardiometabolic disease-free survival than slower or normal agers (Δ​CHA≤0\Delta\text{CHA}\leq 0, n=10,697n=10{,}697; 8-year survival 79.28%79.28\% versus 82.41%82.41\%, log-rank P=7.09×10−6P=7.09\times 10^{-6}; Figure 2b and Extended Data Table 1). In multivariable Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for baseline chronological age, sex, and BMI, each 1-year increase in Δ​CHA\Delta\text{CHA} remained independently associated with higher incident cardiometabolic risk both at baseline (HR=1.02\mathrm{HR}=1.02, 95%​ CI:[1.01,1.04]95\%\text{ CI}:[1.01,1.04], P=2.8×10−4P=2.8\times 10^{-4}; N=14,663N=14{,}663, 1,4021{,}402 events) and in lagged time-varying models where Δ​CHAt−1\Delta\text{CHA}_{t-1} predicted incident diagnosis in the subsequent quarter (HR=1.04\mathrm{HR}=1.04, 95%​ CI:[1.02,1.05]95\%\text{ CI}:[1.02,1.05], P=6.0×10−7P=6.0\times 10^{-7}; N=13,842N=13{,}842, 164,336164{,}336 person-quarters; Extended Data Table 2). Crucially, adding CHA to the clinical baseline of age, sex, and BMI significantly improved prognostic discrimination across the full cohort (Harrell’s C-index 0.65410.6541 versus 0.64850.6485, Δ​C=+0.0056\Delta\text{C}=+0.0056, P=0.005P=0.005), in 5-fold cross-validation (Δ​C=+0.0053\Delta\text{C}=+0.0053, P=0.016P=0.016), and most pronouncedly in adults under 50 years of age (N=7,399N=7{,}399; C-index 0.67620.6762 versus 0.66480.6648, Δ​C=+0.0114\Delta\text{C}=+0.0114, P<0.001P<0.001; Extended Data Table 3 and Supplementary Figure 2).

2.4 Sensor world models learn physiological health trajectories

Estimating an actionable Health Age requires more than measuring an individual’s present physiological state. It requires a model of how that state evolves over time and how predicted trajectories vary with observed behavioral patterns. We therefore developed SensorWM, an action-conditioned sensor world model trained to reconstruct and forecast longitudinal wearable measurements (Figure 3a). SensorWM was pretrained on trajectories from 96,957 research-consented participants, comprising 2.28 million total person-weeks. Each participant was represented as a weekly sequence of physiological states and observable actions. State inputs included cardiovascular (e.g., Heart Rate Variability), cardiopulmonary (e.g., Respiratory Rate), sleep (e.g., Deep sleep minutes), and variability-related (e.g. dispersion) measurements (e.g., Relative Sample SD30), whereas action inputs captured modifiable behaviors, including step count, sleep duration and time spent in cardio-intensity activity (Full Decomposition Breakdowns of Feature Splits in Supplementary Table 6).

SensorWM consists of a physiological state encoder and an action-conditioned transition model. A multilayer perceptron first encodes physiological measurements into a 128-dimensional latent representation. The transition model then predicts how this representation changes over time based on the current physiological state, recent changes in that state, and observed behavioral actions. Specifically, it learns a linear transition operator that updates the latent representation using its recent trajectory. Both components are trained jointly using a self-supervised joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), closely following the training objective of LeWorldModel which models trajectory fidelity and a regularization term Maes et al. (2026).

This state–action formulation enabled SensorWM to predict future physiological states based on both observed behaviors and recent physiological changes, allowing the model to capture not only an individual’s current health status but also the direction and trajectory of their physiological evolution. The resulting architecture supports autoregressive forecasting and the simulation of alternative behavioral scenarios over extended horizons, providing the physiological projections used in downstream counterfactual coaching. Additional details on model architecture, training objectives, and recursive inference are provided in Methods.

We next tested whether generated trajectories retained clinically relevant information. This evaluation is more stringent than minimizing point-wise reconstruction error; a forecast can be numerically close to the observed sequence while erasing weak but medically informative covariation across its learned latent representation. We therefore trained matched downstream classifiers using two settings: (1) observed wearable trajectories, (2) SensorWM-generated trajectories. We then evaluated the two settings across health conditions, laboratory-derived metabolic phenotypes, medication use, behavioral activity and women’s health prediction tasks. Across most downstream prediction tasks, SensorWM-generated trajectories outperformed the pretrained Sensor Foundation Model (SensorFM) and Fitbit features without longitudinal trajectory information (Figure 3c). For example, generated trajectories yielded an AUROC of 0.724 for diabetes compared with 0.643 using SensorFM (p=1.85×10−5p=1.85\times 10^{-5}), 0.692 versus 0.614 for hyperlipidemia (p=9.64×10−10p=9.64\times 10^{-10}), and 0.793 versus 0.753 for hypertension (p=5.85×10−4p=5.85\times 10^{-4}). We next evaluated whether SensorWM preserved the clinical information contained in the true longitudinal Fitbit trajectories. Across these tasks, classification performance from generated trajectories closely followed that obtained from the observed data (Figure 3c), with most comparisons showing no statistically significant differences. For example, generated trajectories yielded an AUROC of 0.724 for diabetes compared with 0.723 using Fitbit observed trajectories (pp=0.7037), 0.692 versus 0.691 for hyperlipidemia, and 0.793 versus 0.796 for hypertension (pp=0.7784). Performance was likewise preserved for HOMA-IR-defined insulin resistance, with an AUROC of 0.760 from generated trajectories compared with 0.780 from observed data (pp=0.2782). These results suggest that SensorWM captures clinically informative longitudinal dynamics while preserving much of the predictive information present in observed wearable trajectories.

We then quantified forecasting accuracy across wearable domains and compared SensorWM with persistence and temporal baselines, including the mean of the preceding one, two, or four weeks, last observation carried forward (LOCF), and the time-series foundation model TimesFM Das et al. (2024). SensorWM was initialized using the first two observed physiological states and subsequently propagated autoregressively, with each physiological state transition conditioned on the corresponding behavioral action vector. The largest improvements occurred for measurements with substantial temporal variation and cross-modal dependence. SensorWM attained R2=0.877R^{2}=0.877 for resting heart rate, compared with 0.705 for last observation carried forward and 0.686 for TimesFM. For heart-rate variability, SensorWM reached R2=0.855R^{2}=0.855, compared with 0.682 and 0.605, respectively. Respiratory rate was forecast with R2=0.884R^{2}=0.884, substantially exceeding last observation carried forward (R2=0.623)(R^{2}=0.623) and TimesFM (R2=0.503)(R^{2}=0.503). SensorWM also performed strongly for time spent in lower-intensity heart-rate zones, achieving R2=0.814R^{2}=0.814 for heart-rate zone 1 minutes and R2=0.826R^{2}=0.826 for activity zone 1 minutes. These features reflect both behavior and physiological response; predicting them therefore requires the model to integrate activity patterns with individual cardiovascular dynamics rather than rely solely on univariate persistence.

2.5 SensorWM enables individualized counterfactual simulation and feasibility-constrained coaching

We next used SensorWM to project how individual physiological trajectories may change under alternative behavioral scenarios. For each participant, SensorWM was initialized from the same recent physiological history and rolled forward for 12 weeks under candidate changes in daily steps, sleep duration, and cardio-intensity activity. Each projected trajectory was decoded into wearable-derived physiological measures and mapped to CHA, allowing alternative model-implied futures to be compared from a common starting state (Figure 4a).

To translate these projections into actionable coaching options, we coupled SensorWM with a feasibility-constrained optimization procedure (Figure 4b, Methods). For each participant, candidate behavioral plans were evaluated according to their projected reduction in CHA and the behavioral effort required to achieve them. Effort was defined relative to the participant’s own recent behavioral variability, such that changes consistent with previously observed behavior were favored over larger departures from their usual range. The resulting candidate plans were ranked to prioritize projected physiological improvement while accounting for participant-specific feasibility.

The coaching engine then applied additional constraints before plan generation (Figure 4c). Only directly modifiable behaviors (daily steps, sleep duration, and cardio-intensity activity) were treated as intervention targets, whereas resting heart rate, other physiological measurements, and CHA remained projected outcomes. Candidate plans were further screened against participant-specific behavioral limits and safety constraints through feasibility-constrained optimization before the highest-ranked scenarios were passed to the coaching model. This design separates actions that a participant can take from physiological responses predicted by SensorWM.

At the individual level, the projected benefits of behavioral interventions remained dependent on physiological context and participant-specific feasibility (Figure 4d). For one representative participant with greater behavioral adherence capacity, feasibility-constrained optimization selected a plan associated with a 2.3-year reduction in Health Age, approaching the maximum projected reduction of 2.9 years. In contrast, for a participant with lower adherence capacity, the optimizer selected a more conservative plan yielding a 1.3-year reduction despite an unconstrained maximum of 6.7 years. These examples illustrate how maximizing projected physiological improvement alone may favor behavioral changes that are difficult to sustain, whereas incorporating individualized feasibility constraints yields more achievable and personalized intervention targets. The simulation and optimization framework identifies candidate behavioral pathways that balance anticipated health benefits against the effort required to achieve them. These ranked trajectories form the physiological basis of the Counterfactual Coaching system. We next evaluated whether providing these projected futures to an LLM-based coach improved the quality, feasibility, and clinical appropriateness of its recommendations relative to coaching based on observed wearable history alone.

2.6 Blinded human evaluation of counterfactual coaching by lifestyle coaches and clinicians

Having established that SensorWM generates individualized, feasibility ranked behavioral trajectories, we evaluated whether incorporating these projections into an LLM coaching agent improved the resulting behavioral prescriptions. We compared Counterfactual Coaching which conditioned the coaching agent on each participant’s baseline CHA, SensorWM-projected wearable trajectory, and feasibility ranked counterfactual pathways against a Generic Coaching baseline that used the identical underlying LLM, participant wearable history, plan structure, and behavior-change instructions, but without CHA or simulation-derived projections.

We conducted a blinded, randomized, dual-track evaluation across 50 cases stratified equally across five prespecified WEAR-ME behavioral personas (49 valid cases after quality control; Figure 5a and Methods). Each paired plan was independently reviewed by five certified lifestyle coaches (assessing overall plan quality, anticipated long-term adherence, and 10 behavioral dimensions) and five board-certified clinicians specializing in primary care or lifestyle medicine (assessing clinical safety gates, physiological accuracy, and 6 clinical dimensions), yielding 245 paired evaluations per track across the 49 valid cases (Figures 1e and 5; Supplementary Information A.3 and Supplementary Tables 26, 27).

In blinded head-to-head comparisons, lifestyle coaches selected Counterfactual Coaching as the best overall plan in 71.4% of evaluations (175/245; 95% CI, 65.5–76.7%; P = 1.49×10−111.49\times 10^{-11}; Figure 5b), compared with 28.6% for Generic Coaching (70/245; two-sided exact binomial P=1.49×10−11P=1.49\times 10^{-11}). Counterfactual Coaching was preferred for anticipated long-term adherence in 71.0% of evaluations (174/245; 95% CI, 65.0–76.3%; P = 3.72×10−113.72\times 10^{-11}; Figure 1e), compared with 29.0% for Generic Coaching (71/245; P=3.72×10−11P=3.72\times 10^{-11}; Figure 1e). Preference direction was uniform across all five lifestyle coaches, with majority rater consensus favoring Counterfactual Coaching in 87.8%87.8\% (43/4943/49) of cases for overall quality and 89.8%89.8\% (44/4944/49) for adherence (Supplementary Table 26). Crucially, these gains did not come at the expense of clinical safety. Clinicians judged 99.2%99.2\% (243/245243/245) of Counterfactual plans and 97.6%97.6\% (239/245239/245) of Generic plans to be within safe exercise intensity limits (P=0.289P=0.289), with comparably high physiological claim accuracy (97.1%97.1\% versus 97.6%97.6\%; Figure 1e and Supplementary Table 27).

Multi-aspect rubric evaluations revealed that overall preference was driven by dimensions directly enabled by counterfactual trajectory modeling (Figure 5b and Supplementary Tables 26, 27). Among lifestyle coaches, Counterfactual plans substantially outperformed Generic plans in contrasting the benefits of behavior change against the status-quo trajectory (73.5%73.5\% versus 5.7%5.7\%; Δ=+67.8\Delta=+67.8 percentage points, P=3.15×10−45P=3.15\times 10^{-45}), providing a compelling reason to change without fear- or shame-based framing (75.5%75.5\% versus 28.6%28.6\%; Δ=+46.9\Delta=+46.9 points), and conveying actionable control over the future trajectory (97.1%97.1\% versus 59.4%59.4\%; Δ=+37.7\Delta=+37.7 points). Counterfactual plans also achieved higher top-box ratings for behavior-change strategies (50.2%50.2\% versus 20.4%20.4\%) and sustainable habit building (52.2%52.2\% versus 28.6%28.6\%), and were more frequently rated realistic and non-overwhelming (98.8%98.8\% versus 82.9%82.9\%) and supportive in tone (98.4%98.4\% versus 83.3%83.3\%), whereas general comprehensibility (84.9%84.9\% versus 89.8%89.8\%, P=0.111P=0.111) and multi-signal synthesis (49.0%49.0\% versus 48.6%48.6\%) were comparable between arms. Clinician evaluations mirrored these findings: clinicians rated Counterfactual plans markedly higher for contrasting intervention benefits against the status quo (92.2%92.2\% versus 7.8%7.8\%; Δ=+84.5\Delta=+84.5 points, P=3.49×10−55P=3.49\times 10^{-55}), baseline physiological personalization (72.2%72.2\% versus 52.2%52.2\%; Δ=+20.0\Delta=+20.0 points, P=5.57×10−6P=5.57\times 10^{-6}), and 12-week biological plausibility (86.1%86.1\% versus 81.6%81.6\%, P=0.043P=0.043). Complementary perspectives between coaches and clinicians, including how clinicians prioritized physiological risk tailoring while coaches emphasized behavioral agency and external lifestyle constraints, are detailed in Supplementary Table 28.

Stratified analyses confirmed that the preference for Counterfactual Coaching generalized across all five WEAR-ME personas (Figure 5c and Supplementary Table 29), led by Multi-Risk Challengers (Persona 2; 80.0%80.0\% win rate, 40/5040/50), Activity Bottleneck (Persona 4; 74.0%74.0\%, 37/5037/50), Optimal Baseline (Persona 1; 72.0%72.0\%, 36/5036/50), and Balanced Maintainers (Persona 5; 71.1%71.1\%, 32/4532/45). Qualitative error analysis and subgroup comparisons also surfaced two interpretable failure modes (Supplementary Table 29): first, in the Recovery Bottleneck persona (P3; high baseline activity but insufficient sleep, 60.0%60.0\% win rate, 30/5030/50), some plans prescribed redundant step increases in an already saturated activity domain; second, in high-risk profiles (P2), clinicians noted that a subset of 12-week CHA reductions (4–5 years) appeared overly optimistic in magnitude, indicating an opportunity for tighter physiological timescale calibration. These dual-track evaluations demonstrate that grounding an LLM coach in SensorWM counterfactual projections produced more actionable and more frequently preferred behavioral plans while maintaining high expert-rated safety across diverse user profiles.

To complement the expert evaluation and assess scalability across a larger sample, we additionally performed an automated evaluation using rubric-aligned LLM autoraters across an expanded participant cohort (Extended Data Tables 5, 6). Consistent with the blinded lifestyle-coach and clinician assessments, automated evaluations consistently favored Counterfactual Coaching over the Generic Coaching baseline across overall plan quality, trajectory control, and physiological personalization, confirming that the benefits of simulation-grounded coaching generalize across the broader cohort.

3 Discussion

In this study, we introduced CHA and embedded it within an end-to-end counterfactual coaching architecture that couples an autoregressive wearable SensorWM with a feasibility constrained coaching agent. Across population cohorts, we demonstrated that CHA, which is constructed entirely from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals passively tracked by consumer wearables, captures cardiometabolic health, providing incremental prognostic value for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and BMI in the All of Us cohort, and within-person behavioral plasticity over time. We further showed that SensorWM accurately forecasts multi-week physiological trajectories across coupled wearable signals, outperforming generic time series foundation models and statistical baselines while generating biologically coherent counterfactual rollouts under candidate lifestyle modifications. Crucially, in a blinded, dual-track evaluation by certified lifestyle coaches and board-certified clinicians, conditioning an LLM coaching agent on CHA and SensorWM counterfactual trajectories substantially improved overall plan quality and projected long-term adherence compared with coaching grounded in retrospective wearable data alone, while maintaining high clinical safety and physiological plausibility.

A central methodological challenge in quantifying biological aging is the absence of a single gold-standard ground truth Moqri et al. (2023). Because true biological age is latent, we evaluated CHA through its alignment with established cardiometabolic constructs, its prospective association with incident disease onset in the All of Us cohort, and its longitudinal sensitivity within individuals. Across academia and industry, prior efforts to quantify biological and physiological aging span four primary paradigms, each confronting a fundamental trade-off between clinical validity and everyday behavioral actionability. First, at the molecular and clinical level, epigenetic, proteomic, and blood panel clocks, evolving from first generation chronological age predictors Horvath (2013); Hannum et al. (2013) to second generation mortality clocks (PhenoAge Levine et al. (2018); GrimAge Lu et al. (2019); McCrory et al. (2021)), third generation longitudinal pace of aging biomarkers (DunedinPACE Belsky et al. (2022)), and clinical blood composites, Klemera and Ďoubal (2006); Segterra, Inc. (2021)capture deep cellular and systemic senescence, yet their reliance on invasive, costly, and episodic sampling limits their utility as high frequency feedback signals for daily behavior change. Second, classical epidemiological risk age models, such as Framingham Vascular/Heart Age D’Agostino Sr et al. (2008), Spiegelhalter’s effective age formulation Spiegelhalter (2016), and commercial actuarial engines (Vitality Age), translate multivariable proportional hazards into intuitive age equivalents, but operate as static, episodic snapshots. Third, earlier wearable-based age estimators trained to regress chronological time Pyrkov et al. (2018); Miller et al. (2025) often latch onto age correlated features that carry limited prognostic or modifiable signal, as reflected in their weak concordance with clinical reference scores in our benchmarks. Fourth, commercial consumer wearable features have largely traded multi system clinical disease grounding for convenience: Garmin Fitness Age maps cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2​max\text{VO}_{2}\text{max}) and resting heart rate against population percentiles without linking to clinical disease incidence Garmin Ltd. (2021); Oura Cardiovascular Age Ōura Health (2024) and polysomnographic Sleep Age models Brink-Kjaer et al. (2022) infer physiological age from passive photoplethysmography (pulse wave velocity) or sleep waveforms, offering observational state readouts that cannot be causally decomposed into specific behavioral targets; and WHOOP Healthspan (WHOOP Age and Pace of Aging WHOOP Inc. and Buck Institute for Research on Aging (2025)) aggregates lifestyle exposures using hazard ratios parameterized on late life all cause mortality rather than earlier onset cardiometabolic morbidity.

Our framework resolves this validity–actionability tension by unifying epidemiological survival modeling, action-conditioned trajectory forecasting, and counterfactual behavioral AI coaching agent into a modular, closed-loop architecture. Rather than regressing chronological age, matching population fitness percentiles, or awaiting late life mortality endpoints, CHA anchors high frequency wearable signals directly to published epidemiological hazard ratios for incident cardiometabolic diseases, the earliest and most modifiable burden of chronic morbidity prioritizing time varying behavioral features across physical activity, sedentary patterns, sleep regularity, and cardiorespiratory health, consistent with preventive frameworks such as Life’s Essential 8 Lloyd-Jones et al. (2022). By design, this hazard ratio formulation is inherently extensible: unlike monolithic end to end machine learning clocks that require complete retraining when inputs change, new behavioral signals, wearable sensors, or clinical biomarkers (e.g., resistance training volume, dietary patterns, or continuous glucose metrics) can be seamlessly incorporated as new epidemiological evidence or sensing modalities emerge. Expressing these multi-system risks on a shared age equivalent scale yields a responsive metric through which individuals can track their physiological state over time and transparently inspect which factors drive it. Finally, instead of treating Health Age as a static assessment, we pair CHA with an action conditioned trajectory prediction model and a counterfactual coaching agent that operates directly on the user’s interpretable behavioral state space, solving for feasible, personalized habit adjustments that yield the greatest marginal reduction in cardiometabolic disease hazard and actively guide the individual toward a younger physiological trajectory.

Our work also advances recent efforts applying large language models and foundation models to biological aging and personal health coaching. Recently, Li et al. demonstrated that LLMs can estimate system-wide and organ-specific biological age directly from routine physical examination records and clinical biomarkers across large-scale populations Li et al. (2025). While such approaches highlight the capacity of LLMs to synthesize cross-sectional clinical records for static risk stratification, direct zero-shot LLM estimation of health age from continuous wearable streams showed substantially lower alignment with clinical cardiometabolic references in our evaluations. Similarly, recent wearable-grounded conversational agents, including PH-LLM and multi-agent personal health frameworks Khasentino et al. (2025); Merrill et al. (2026); Heydari et al. (2025) have established important benchmarks for interpreting retrospective sensor summaries, yet they rely on the language model’s qualitative priors to prescribe behavioral changes. Our architecture bridges these paradigms by separating physiological state estimation and trajectory simulation from natural-language synthesis. Rather than asking an LLM to implicitly guess both biological age and future intervention responses, we pair an explicit, interpretable health age target (i.e., CHA) with a dedicated quantitative world model (i.e., SensorWM) and validate the resulting prescriptions through dual lifestyle-coaching and clinical expert tracks.

This architectural separation directly addresses the explainability gap in clinical artificial intelligence, where post-hoc attribution methods typically identify which inputs drove a static risk score without indicating how an individual can alter that trajectory Ghassemi et al. (2021); Kumar et al. (2020); Karimi et al. (2021). In our framework, component-level age attributions in CHA are directly coupled to SensorWM’s action-conditioned rollouts, translating static feature importance into concrete, quantified behavioral levers such as how a specific increase in daily steps, or sleep duration is projected to shift an individual’s future Health Age. The impact of this design was directly reflected in our expert evaluations: the largest advantages of Counterfactual Coaching over Generic Coaching emerged precisely in contrasting projected intervention benefits against a trajectory of continued current habits (Δ=+67.8\Delta=+67.8 percentage points among coaches; Δ=+84.5\Delta=+84.5 points among clinicians), providing a compelling rationale for change, and fostering perceived control over one’s health trajectory. Explainability, when operationalized through prospective outcome projections rather than retrospective attributions, thus serves as an active mechanism for motivational framing and sustainable habit formation.

A key technical contribution of this study is demonstrating that a domain specific Sensor World Model can learn coupled, multi week physiological dynamics across behavioral inputs and physiological responses (such as resting heart rate and physical activity), outperforming general purpose time series foundation models across forecasting horizons. Simulating "what-if" behavioral scenarios over a 12-week horizon enabled the coaching agent to evaluate candidate regimens against individualized feasibility constraints before recommending a single goal to the user.

Our dual-track human evaluation yielded important insights into both the strengths and current failure modes of simulation guided coaching, as well as how different domain experts evaluate AI-generated coaching advice. While both expert panels strongly favored Counterfactual Coaching overall and confirmed its high safety (99.2%99.2\% within safe intensity bounds), lifestyle coaches and clinicians prioritized distinct dimensions of personalization. Clinicians were particularly sensitive to physiological risk tailoring and the contrast between projected intervention benefits and the continued current habits, whereas lifestyle coaches focused heavily on behavioral agency, habit progression, and real-world barriers beyond wearable sensors noting in qualitative feedback that wearable derived personalization does not yet capture work schedules, caregiving duties, or environmental access. Furthermore, persona stratified error analyses highlighted two actionable failure modes: in already highly active users with sleep deficits (Recovery Bottleneck), the optimizer occasionally suggested redundant step increases alongside sleep goals; and in high-risk profiles (Multi-Risk Challengers), clinicians flagged a subset of 4–5 year projected CHA reductions over 12 weeks as overly optimistic, underscoring the need to constrain not only behavioral input feasibility but also the biological rate of physiological adaptation.

Our findings point toward a scalable paradigm for preventive medicine, primary care, and population health management. Because CHA and SensorWM operate entirely on passive signals from widely adopted consumer wearables, this framework can function as a continuous digital companion between episodic clinic visits identifying subclinical cardiometabolic drift early and translating longitudinal risk into individualized, clinician auditable lifestyle prescriptions. In primary care and lifestyle medicine workflows, presenting patients with an intuitive age equivalent metric alongside personalized "what-if" trajectories could enhance shared decision making, replace generic lifestyle handouts with tailored 12-week action plans, and enable remote monitoring of physiological response to prescribed habits. Prospective randomized controlled trials will be needed to determine whether deploying counterfactual wearable coaching in real-world populations leads to sustained behavioral adherence, durable reductions in CHA, and measurable improvements in long-term cardiometabolic outcomes.

Several limitations of this study warrant consideration and inform directions for future work. First, although SensorWM captures longitudinal temporal dynamics across behavioral and physiological signals, it is trained on observational wearable data rather than randomized interventional trials; consequently, its counterfactual projections reflect conditional observational associations rather than guaranteed causal treatment effects, and unmeasured time varying factors such as dietary changes, medication adjustments, intercurrent illness, or psychosocial stress may confound observed trajectories. Second, while consumer wearables enable passive, high frequency monitoring, wearable-owning cohorts can reflect socioeconomic and health conscious selection biases, and wrist worn sensors do not directly measure nutritional intake, resistance training load, or contextual barriers to behavior change such as work schedules, caregiving responsibilities, and environmental access. Third, whereas candidate sleep targets in the counterfactual grid were capped at 9 hours, we did not impose an upper saturation cap on candidate daily step targets because additional step volume can still influence projected downstream physiology such as resting heart rate and Active Zone Minutes through SensorWM; however, in already highly active individuals with insufficient sleep (Recovery Bottleneck), this design choice occasionally led the optimizer to propose further step increases alongside sleep goals, suggesting that future implementations should incorporate baseline-aware saturation ceilings or diminishing-return constraints in the candidate action grid. Finally, we evaluated coaching plans using blinded reviews by clinicians and lifestyle coaches, which is an essential step before deploying AI recommendations to users. A natural next step will be to follow users over time to measure how these plans affect real-world habit adherence and CHA.

4 Methods

4.1 Coachable Health Age

4.1.1 Health Age formulation

CHA was designed to summarize health on an age-equivalent scale using physiological and behavioral characteristics that can be repeatedly measured with consumer wearables and that have established associations with adverse health outcomes. In contrast to wearable age models trained to recover chronological age, CHA was not optimized to predict elapsed time. Instead, each constituent measurement was mapped to a relative-risk contribution using published epidemiological associations, and the resulting risk contributions were expressed in age-equivalent units Spiegelhalter (2016).

For participant jj, the Health Age Delta was defined as

Δ​Agej=1G​∑i=1Kwi​log⁡(HRi​j),\Delta\mathrm{Age}_{j}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}\log\left(\mathrm{HR}_{ij}\right), (1)

where HRi​j\mathrm{HR}_{ij} denotes the relative hazard ratio associated with health domain ii for participant jj, wiw_{i} denotes the corresponding weight in log-hazard space, and G=0.1G=0.1 is an age-rate constant approximating a 10% exponential increase in mortality risk per year of age. CHA was then

HealthAgej=Agejchronological+Δ​Agej.\mathrm{HealthAge}_{j}=\mathrm{Age}^{\mathrm{chronological}}_{j}+\Delta\mathrm{Age}_{j}. (2)

Thus, Δ​Age>0\Delta\mathrm{Age}>0 denotes a Health Age older than chronological age and Δ​Age<0\Delta\mathrm{Age}<0 denotes a Health Age younger than chronological age.

The primary wearable-derived components were resting heart rate, mean daily step count, mean sleep duration, and weekly Active Zone Minutes (AZM). Cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2​max\mathrm{VO}_{2}\max), wearable-predicted insulin resistance, and sleep regularity were incorporated as optional components when available. Resting heart rate was mapped using published associations with incident heart-failure risk Zhang et al. (2016); daily step count using associations with incident diabetes Master et al. (2022); sleep duration using a U-shaped association with cardiovascular disease Daghlas et al. (2019); and weekly AZM using reported associations between physical-activity volume and cardiovascular risk Kany et al. (2024); Wei et al. (2026). Cardiorespiratory fitness was represented relative to age-, sex-, and weight-expected VO2​max\mathrm{VO}_{2}\max and mapped using reported mortality associations per metabolic equivalent Mandsager et al. (2018). Sleep regularity was quantified using the standard deviation of sleep midpoint and mapped using reported associations between sleep irregularity and cardiovascular risk Huang et al. (2020). Predicted insulin resistance was obtained from a previously validated wearable and demographic prediction model Metwally et al. (2026).

Because the four primary wearable-derived quantities (daily steps, weekly AZM, resting heart rate, and sleep duration) encode correlated aspects of activity, autonomic tone, and sleep, summing their unadjusted literature log-hazards with unit weights would double-count shared risk variance. To account for multicollinearity among these four core domains, we estimated the empirical correlation matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} of their log-hazard contributions in the WEAR-ME cohort and solved for mutually adjusted weights 𝐰=𝐑−1​𝟏\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{1} in standardized log-hazard space, yielding wsleep=0.8790w_{\mathrm{sleep}}=0.8790, wRHR=0.7066w_{\mathrm{RHR}}=0.7066, wAZM=0.6950w_{\mathrm{AZM}}=0.6950, and wsteps=0.4773w_{\mathrm{steps}}=0.4773 in Eq. (1) (with wi=1.0w_{i}=1.0 for the optional domains when available).

4.1.2 Detailed parameterization of CHA: core wearable domains

CHA converts each constituent wearable or physiological measurement to a log-relative-risk contribution log⁡(HRi)\log(\mathrm{HR}_{i}) and aggregates these contributions using the domain weights wiw_{i} according to Eq. (1) Spiegelhalter (2016).

4.1.2.1 Resting heart rate.

Resting heart rate was mapped using reported associations with incident heart-failure risk Zhang et al. (2016), with RHR≤60​ bpm\mathrm{RHR}\leq 60\text{ bpm} as the reference region (HR=1.0\mathrm{HR}=1.0):

log⁡(HRRHR)={0,RHR≤60,RHR−6010​log⁡(1.08),60<RHR≤70,log⁡(1.08)+RHR−7020​[log⁡(1.33)−log⁡(1.08)],RHR>70.\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{RHR}})=\begin{cases}0,&\mathrm{RHR}\leq 60,\\[4.0pt] \dfrac{\mathrm{RHR}-60}{10}\log(1.08),&60<\mathrm{RHR}\leq 70,\\[10.0pt] \log(1.08)+\dfrac{\mathrm{RHR}-70}{20}\left[\log(1.33)-\log(1.08)\right],&\mathrm{RHR}>70.\end{cases} (3)
4.1.2.2 Daily steps.

Daily step count was mapped using reported associations between daily steps and incident diabetes Master et al. (2022), with a reference of 8,000​ steps/day8{,}000\text{ steps/day} (HR=1.0\mathrm{HR}=1.0) and an upper plateau at Stepseff=min⁡(Steps,9000)\mathrm{Steps}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\min(\mathrm{Steps},9000):

log⁡(HRsteps)=min⁡(Steps,9000)−80001000​log⁡(0.88).\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{steps}})=\frac{\min(\mathrm{Steps},9000)-8000}{1000}\log(0.88). (4)
4.1.2.3 Sleep duration.

Sleep duration was mapped using the reported U-shaped association with incident cardiovascular disease Daghlas et al. (2019), with 6.0​–​9.0​ hours/night6.0\text{--}9.0\text{ hours/night} as the optimal reference interval (HR=1.0\mathrm{HR}=1.0):

log⁡(HRsleep)={(6.0−Sleep)​log⁡(1.20),Sleep<6.0,0,6.0≤Sleep≤9.0,(Sleep−9.0)​log⁡(1.34),Sleep>9.0.\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{sleep}})=\begin{cases}(6.0-\mathrm{Sleep})\log(1.20),&\mathrm{Sleep}<6.0,\\[4.0pt] 0,&6.0\leq\mathrm{Sleep}\leq 9.0,\\[4.0pt] (\mathrm{Sleep}-9.0)\log(1.34),&\mathrm{Sleep}>9.0.\end{cases} (5)
4.1.2.4 Active Zone Minutes.

Weekly AZM was mapped using reported quartile associations between moderate-to-vigorous physical-activity volume and cardiovascular risk Kany et al. (2024); Wei et al. (2026), with <115​ minutes/week<115\text{ minutes/week} as the reference baseline (HR=1.0\mathrm{HR}=1.0) and a plateau at ≥500​ minutes/week\geq 500\text{ minutes/week}:

log⁡(HRAZM)={0,AZM<115,AZM−115130​log⁡(0.76),115≤AZM<245,log⁡(0.76)+AZM−245173​[log⁡(0.71)−log⁡(0.76)],245≤AZM<418,log⁡(0.71)+AZM−41882​[log⁡(0.68)−log⁡(0.71)],418≤AZM<500,log⁡(0.68),AZM≥500.\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{AZM}})=\begin{cases}0,&\mathrm{AZM}<115,\\[5.0pt] \dfrac{\mathrm{AZM}-115}{130}\log(0.76),&115\leq\mathrm{AZM}<245,\\[10.0pt] \log(0.76)+\dfrac{\mathrm{AZM}-245}{173}\left[\log(0.71)-\log(0.76)\right],&245\leq\mathrm{AZM}<418,\\[10.0pt] \log(0.71)+\dfrac{\mathrm{AZM}-418}{82}\left[\log(0.68)-\log(0.71)\right],&418\leq\mathrm{AZM}<500,\\[10.0pt] \log(0.68),&\mathrm{AZM}\geq 500.\end{cases} (6)

4.1.3 Multicollinearity weights (wiw_{i}) calibrated in the WEAR-ME cohort

To estimate the domain weights wiw_{i} in Eq. (1) without double-counting shared physiological variance across correlated wearable domains, we first evaluated the four unadjusted log-hazard contributions log⁡(HRsleep)\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{sleep}}), log⁡(HRRHR)\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{RHR}}), log⁡(HRsteps)\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{steps}}), and log⁡(HRAZM)\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{AZM}}) across participants in the WEAR-ME cohort using Eqs. (3)–(6). Evaluating correlations in transformed log-hazard space rather than on raw wearable variables is necessary because raw sleep duration has a non-monotonic U-shaped relationship with mortality risk, and daily steps, RHR, and AZM contain saturation plateaus; in log-hazard space, all four domains are aligned on a common monotonic risk scale.

Because the published hazard ratios originate from independent studies with distinct clinical endpoints and covariate adjustments, rather than univariate regressions against a single outcome in a single cohort, applying an unstandardized covariance inversion (𝚺−1​𝝈2\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2}) would weight off-diagonal adjustments by the ratio of domain standard deviations (σk/σi\sigma_{k}/\sigma_{i}), allowing domains with wide numerical ranges (such as daily steps) to over-subtract from narrower-range physiological domains (such as RHR). To discount each domain strictly according to its empirical informational overlap with the remaining domains, we standardized each log-hazard column to unit variance, computed the 4×44\times 4 Pearson correlation matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} across the WEAR-ME cohort (Ri​k=Corr⁡(log⁡HRi,log⁡HRk)R_{ik}=\mathrm{Corr}(\log\mathrm{HR}_{i},\log\mathrm{HR}_{k})), and solved the standardized linear system for the domain weights 𝐰\mathbf{w}:

𝐑𝐰~=𝟏⟺𝐰~=𝐑−1𝟏,wi=min(max(w~i,0), 1).\mathbf{R}\tilde{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{1}\hskip 10.00002pt\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{1},\hskip 20.00003ptw_{i}=\min\!\left(\max(\tilde{w}_{i},0),\,1\right). (7)

In Eq. (7), each domain’s unit marginal weight (1.01.0) is decomposed into its unique direct weight wiw_{i} plus its correlated overlap with the other domains (∑k≠iRi​k​wk\sum_{k\neq i}R_{ik}w_{k}). Estimating Eq. (7) on the WEAR-ME cohort yielded the weights:

wsleep=0.8790,wRHR=0.7066,wAZM=0.6950,wsteps=0.4773.w_{\mathrm{sleep}}=0.8790,\hskip 20.00003ptw_{\mathrm{RHR}}=0.7066,\hskip 20.00003ptw_{\mathrm{AZM}}=0.6950,\hskip 20.00003ptw_{\mathrm{steps}}=0.4773. (8)

Multiplying each core domain’s log-hazard contribution by wiw_{i} in Eq. (1) scales each knot log-hazard coefficient from βi=log⁡(HRi)\beta_{i}=\log(\mathrm{HR}_{i}) to βiadj=wi​log⁡(HRi)=log⁡(HRiwi)\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{i}=w_{i}\log(\mathrm{HR}_{i})=\log(\mathrm{HR}_{i}^{w_{i}}), which is equivalent to replacing each unadjusted knot hazard ratio HRi\mathrm{HR}_{i} in Eqs. (3)–(6) with its collinearity-adjusted hazard ratio:

log(HRiadj)=wilog(HRi)⟺HRiadj=exp(wilogHRi)=(HRi)wi.\log\!\left(\mathrm{HR}^{\mathrm{adj}}_{i}\right)=w_{i}\log\!\left(\mathrm{HR}_{i}\right)\hskip 10.00002pt\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 10.00002pt\mathrm{HR}^{\mathrm{adj}}_{i}=\exp\!\left(w_{i}\log\mathrm{HR}_{i}\right)=\left(\mathrm{HR}_{i}\right)^{w_{i}}. (9)

This formulation guarantees that all reference baselines remain invariant (1.0wi=1.01.0^{w_{i}}=1.0, log⁡HRiadj=0\log\mathrm{HR}^{\mathrm{adj}}_{i}=0) and preserves exact piecewise continuity at all interior knots. Supplementary Table 1 summarizes the unadjusted literature hazard ratios, the WEAR-ME weights wiw_{i}, and the resulting collinearity-adjusted knot hazard ratios HRiadj\mathrm{HR}^{\mathrm{adj}}_{i}.

When available for a participant, the following three domains are evaluated with weight wi=1.0w_{i}=1.0 (defaulting to wi=0w_{i}=0 when any required input is unmeasured):

4.1.4.1 Cardiorespiratory fitness.

When measured run VO2​max\mathrm{VO}_{2}\max (mL⋅kg−1⋅min−1\text{mL}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\cdot\text{min}^{-1}), biological sex (Female=1\mathrm{Female}=1 for female, 00 for male), and body weight (Weightlb\mathrm{Weight}_{\mathrm{lb}}, in pounds) are available, expected fitness is computed via the FRIEND registry equation Mandsager et al. (2018):
