and mapped to a log-hazard contribution:

log⁡(HRVO2)=(VO2,measured−VO2​max^3.5)​log⁡(0.88).\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{VO_{2}}})=\left(\frac{\mathrm{VO}_{2,\mathrm{measured}}-\widehat{\mathrm{VO}_{2}\max}}{3.5}\right)\log(0.88). (11)
4.1.4.2 Sleep regularity.

When the standard deviation of sleep midpoint (SDmidpoint\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{midpoint}}, in minutes) is available, it is capped at SDeff=min⁡(SDmidpoint,120)\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\min(\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{midpoint}},120) and mapped Huang et al. (2020) with ≤30​ minutes\leq 30\text{ minutes} as the reference region:

log⁡(HRregularity)={0,SDeff≤30,SDeff−3030​log⁡(1.16),30<SDeff≤60,log⁡(1.16)+SDeff−6030​[log⁡(1.52)−log⁡(1.16)],60<SDeff≤90,log⁡(1.52)+SDeff−9030​[log⁡(2.11)−log⁡(1.52)],SDeff>90.\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{regularity}})=\begin{cases}0,&\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq 30,\\[5.0pt] \dfrac{\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{eff}}-30}{30}\log(1.16),&30<\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq 60,\\[10.0pt] \log(1.16)+\dfrac{\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{eff}}-60}{30}\left[\log(1.52)-\log(1.16)\right],&60<\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq 90,\\[10.0pt] \log(1.52)+\dfrac{\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{eff}}-90}{30}\left[\log(2.11)-\log(1.52)\right],&\mathrm{SD}_{\mathrm{eff}}>90.\end{cases} (12)
4.1.4.3 Insulin resistance.

When wearable-predicted insulin-resistance status Metwally et al. (2026) is available, it contributes

log⁡(HRIR)={log⁡(2.00),IR=True,0,IR=False.\log(\mathrm{HR}_{\mathrm{IR}})=\begin{cases}\log(2.00),&\mathrm{IR}=\mathrm{True},\\ 0,&\mathrm{IR}=\mathrm{False}.\end{cases} (13)

4.1.5 Mathematical saturation and CHA plateau

Because each core physiological metric and health behavior within our framework incorporates discrete plateaus, right-censored saturation thresholds, or bounded reference ranges, the resulting CHA models naturally exhibit structural ceilings on maximum age reduction. In the unadjusted 4-metric CHA model, an individual can only achieve the maximum possible age reduction—capped at 5.13​ years5.13\text{ years} younger than chronological age (Δ​Age=−5.135​ years\Delta\text{Age}=-5.135\text{ years})—if they simultaneously optimize all four digital inputs. This requires maintaining a resting heart rate (RHR) ≤60​ bpm\leq 60\text{ bpm} (reference risk level, HR=1.00\text{HR}=1.00, 0.00​ years0.00\text{ years}), reaching or exceeding 9,000​ daily steps9{,}000\text{ daily steps} (capping the step HR at 0.880.88, or −1.28​ years-1.28\text{ years} relative to the 8,0008{,}000-step baseline), sleeping between 6.06.0 and 9.0​ hours9.0\text{ hours} per night (avoiding U-shaped short- and long-sleep penalties, HR=1.00\text{HR}=1.00, 0.00​ years0.00\text{ years}), and logging ≥500​ weekly Active Zone Minutes\geq 500\text{ weekly Active Zone Minutes} (AZM; capping the AZM HR at 0.680.68, or −3.86​ years-3.86\text{ years}). Because further behavioral extensions (e.g., 20,000​ steps/day20{,}000\text{ steps/day} or 1,000​ AZM/week1{,}000\text{ AZM/week}) encounter explicit log-hazard plateaus rooted in epidemiological saturation points, the formulation mathematically prevents an individual from bypassing this lifestyle-driven rejuvenation floor through extreme volume in a single behavior.

In the collinearity-corrected CHA model, attenuating the marginal hazard ratios to account for physiological and behavioral overlap across the four core wearable metrics tightens this structural rejuvenation cap from −5.13​ years-5.13\text{ years} to −3.29​ years-3.29\text{ years} (Δ​Age=−3.292​ years\Delta\text{Age}=-3.292\text{ years}). Under collinearity correction, RHR (≤60​ bpm\leq 60\text{ bpm}) and sleep duration (6.0​–​9.0​ hours6.0\text{--}9.0\text{ hours}) remain neutral reference anchors (0.00​ years0.00\text{ years}), while the maximum achievable reductions from daily steps (≥9,000​ steps/day\geq 9{,}000\text{ steps/day}, HRcorr=0.9408\text{HR}_{\text{corr}}=0.9408) and weekly AZM (≥500​ mins/week\geq 500\text{ mins/week}, HRcorr=0.7648\text{HR}_{\text{corr}}=0.7648) attenuate to −0.61​ years-0.61\text{ years} and −2.68​ years-2.68\text{ years}, respectively. When the extended optional metrics are incorporated into the collinearity-corrected model, sleep midpoint consistency (≤30​ min SD\leq 30\text{ min SD}) and insulin resistance status (absent) operate strictly as unidirectional risk penalties (0.00​ years0.00\text{ years} when optimal, adding up to +7.47​ years+7.47\text{ years} at ≥120​ min SD\geq 120\text{ min SD} and +6.93​ years+6.93\text{ years} when insulin resistant) and therefore do not expand the maximum age reduction. Only the optional cardiorespiratory fitness term (VO2​ max\text{VO}_{2}\text{ max}) is modeled continuously without an upper saturation plateau, conferring an additional −1.28​ years-1.28\text{ years} of age reduction (HR=0.88\text{HR}=0.88) for each 1.0​ MET1.0\text{ MET} (3.5​ mL⋅kg−1⋅min−13.5\text{ mL}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\cdot\text{min}^{-1}) achieved above age-, sex-, and weight-predicted norms, subject only to a global lower bound of 18.0​ years18.0\text{ years} on final Health Age.

4.1.6 Standard health and risk scores

We evaluated whether CHA captured clinically meaningful variation using two complementary reference measures of cardiovascular and metabolic health: a modified Life’s Essential 8 score and the Metabolic Syndrome Severity Score. Neither reference measure was used to fit CHA.

4.1.6.1 Modified Life’s Essential 8.

We calculated a modified version of the American Heart Association Life’s Essential 8 cardiovascular-health score Lloyd-Jones et al. (2022). Standard Life’s Essential 8 integrates diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep, body mass index, blood lipids, blood glucose, and blood pressure. Because standardized dietary-intake information was unavailable, we omitted the diet component and calculated a seven-component score, hereafter referred to as mod-LE8.

Physical activity was quantified from wearable-derived AZM; sleep health from wearable-measured sleep duration; nicotine exposure from self-report; BMI from clinical measurements; blood pressure from clinical systolic and diastolic measurements together with treatment status; blood lipids from non-HDL cholesterol and lipid-lowering treatment status; and blood glucose from HbA1c and diabetes history. Each component was mapped to a 0–100 cardiovascular-health score according to the corresponding Life’s Essential 8 framework Lloyd-Jones et al. (2022), and mod-LE8 was calculated as the unweighted arithmetic mean of the seven available components. Higher values indicate more favorable cardiovascular health. Additional scoring details are provided in Section 4.1.12.

4.1.6.2 Metabolic Syndrome Severity Score.

We quantified metabolic risk using the continuous Metabolic Syndrome Severity Score (MSSS), following the continuous latent-variable framework established using confirmatory factor analysis Gurka et al. (2014). MSSS combines body mass index, systolic blood pressure, fasting plasma glucose, triglycerides, and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Scores were standardized as sex- and race/ethnicity-specific zz-scores, with higher values indicating greater metabolic-syndrome severity. Participants missing one or more of the five required clinical measurements were excluded from the MSSS analysis.

4.1.7 Construct alignment, comparator benchmarks, and longitudinal modifiability

To evaluate whether CHA reflects current cardiometabolic health more faithfully than alternative age formulations, we benchmarked CHA against chronological age, blood-based Phenotypic Age (PhenoAge), a wearable chronological-age prediction model, and direct LLM-derived health-age estimates. PhenoAge was calculated according to the mortality-risk formulation of Levine et al. Levine et al. (2018). The wearable chronological-age comparator used embeddings from a pretrained Sensor Foundation Model (SensorFM) Narayanswamy et al. (2026), followed by chronological-age regression and correction for the age-dependent regression-to-the-mean bias characteristic of age-prediction models Smith et al. (2019). Direct LLM health-age comparators were generated by prompting the base language model with either the curated CHA feature set or the full set of wearable features. The comparator implementations are described in Section 4.1.13.

Construct alignment with established cardiometabolic reference scores was assessed by calculating Pearson correlation coefficients between each age measure and modified Life’s Essential 8 (mod-LE8) and Metabolic Syndrome Severity Score (MSSS) in the WEAR-ME cohort. Because higher mod-LE8 scores indicate more favorable cardiovascular health whereas higher MSSS scores indicate greater metabolic risk, absolute correlation magnitudes (|r||r|) were used to compare alignment across age formulations (Supplementary Figure 1). We additionally evaluated whether Δ​CHA\Delta\text{CHA} (Health Age minus chronological age) varied systematically across participant-reported overall health categories (from excellent to poor) by computing category-specific means and 95% confidence intervals, comparing separation against age deltas from the wearable chronological-age model.

To characterize within-person longitudinal modifiability, CHA was computed across eight consecutive three-month windows (Q1–Q8; 24 months total) among N=1,464N=1{,}464 participants in the longitudinal Fitbit cohort (Figure 2c). For each participant jj and quarterly window t∈{1,…,8}t\in\{1,\dots,8\}, we computed the health-age delta as

Δ​CHAj,t=CHAj,t−Agej,tchronological,\Delta\mathrm{CHA}_{j,t}=\mathrm{CHA}_{j,t}-\mathrm{Age}^{\mathrm{chronological}}_{j,t}, (14)

and quantified longitudinal shifts relative to baseline (Δ​CHAj,t−Δ​CHAj,1\Delta\mathrm{CHA}_{j,t}-\Delta\mathrm{CHA}_{j,1}), stratifying participants into improved (Δ≤−1​ year\Delta\leq-1\text{ year}), stable (|Δ|<1​ year|\Delta|<1\text{ year}), and deteriorated (Δ≥+1​ year\Delta\geq+1\text{ year}) trajectory groups. These observational analyses characterize natural within-participant plasticity in CHA over coaching-relevant timescales and are not interpreted as causal effects of isolated behavioral interventions.

4.1.8 Prospective validation in the All of Us Research Program

We independently evaluated the prospective association and prognostic utility of CHA for incident cardiometabolic disease using the All of Us Research Program. Participants were required to have at least 730 days of Fitbit tracking span in the daily activity-summary table and at least one valid 90-day wearable window, yielding a total wearable cohort of N=22,748N=22{,}748 participants (276,378276{,}378 three-month windows; 68,101.468{,}101.4 person-years of active wearable tracking; Table 1). Participant sex and year of birth were obtained from the OMOP person table. Baseline BMI was obtained from the OMOP measurement table (concept ID 3038553, restricted to physiologically plausible values of 12​–​80​ kg/m212\text{--}80\text{ kg/m}^{2}) by selecting the measurement closest to the start of wearable tracking, prioritizing measurements recorded on or before the end of the 90-day baseline window. Cardiometabolic outcomes were identified from OMOP condition_occurrence records using the OMOP concept_ancestor hierarchy. Hypertension was defined using ancestor concept ID 316866, type 2 diabetes using ancestor concept ID 201820, and cardiovascular disease using ancestor concept IDs 316139, 4329847, 4182210, and 381591. The composite cardiometabolic outcome was defined as the earliest recorded diagnosis of any of these three conditions. Participants with a recorded diagnosis of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or cardiovascular disease on or prior to the end of their baseline wearable window were excluded from incident-disease survival analyses, leaving 18,42318{,}423 disease-free participants in the primary incident-risk cohort.

4.1.8.1 Wearable aggregation and data-quality criteria.

Daily step count, fairly active minutes, and very active minutes were obtained from Fitbit activity-summary records. Main-sleep duration was derived from daily sleep-summary records restricted to the primary sleep episode (is_main_sleep = TRUE). Minute-level heart-rate records were aggregated to derive daily minimum heart rate (used as the resting heart rate proxy) and the 90th percentile of daily heart rate. A seven-day period was considered valid when at least two days contained complete activity, sleep, and heart-rate measurements. Consecutive 90-day (one-quarter) analysis windows were retained only when they contained at least five distinct valid weeks. Within each retained 90-day window, we calculated mean daily steps, mean main-sleep duration, mean daily minimum heart rate, and mean weekly active zone minutes (defined as fairly active minutes plus twice the very active minutes). CHA and Health Age Delta (Δ​Age=Health​Age−Chronological​Age\Delta\mathrm{Age}=\mathrm{Health\ Age}-\mathrm{Chronological\ Age}) were calculated for each 90-day window.

4.1.9 Baseline Health Age by incident disease status and disease-free survival

We first compared baseline Health Age Delta (mean ±\pm 95% CI) between participants who remained free of all three conditions throughout follow-up (healthy controls) and those who subsequently developed incident hypertension, incident cardiovascular disease, or incident type 2 diabetes after baseline. Next, we tested whether baseline Health Age Delta stratified longitudinal cardiometabolic disease-free survival across the primary incident-risk cohort (N=18,423N=18{,}423). Participants were stratified at baseline into Slower/Normal Agers (Δ​Age≤0\Delta\mathrm{Age}\leq 0; n=10,697n=10{,}697) and Accelerated Agers (Δ​Age>0\Delta\mathrm{Age}>0; n=7,726n=7{,}726). Kaplan–Meier estimators were used to estimate the probability of remaining free of the composite cardiometabolic outcome from the end of the baseline window until the earliest recorded diagnosis of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or cardiovascular disease, or censoring at the end of available wearable follow-up. Disease-free survival probabilities and 95% confidence intervals were evaluated at 4, 8, 16, 24, and 32 quarters (corresponding to 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 years of follow-up; Extended Data Table 1).

4.1.10 Time-varying Cox proportional hazards analysis

To evaluate whether longitudinal Health Age Delta remained independently associated with incident cardiometabolic disease after accounting for demographic and clinical confounders, we fitted a time-varying Cox proportional hazards model. To preserve temporal ordering and mitigate reverse causation from subclinical disease during the same interval, Health Age Delta was lagged by one 90-day window so that Δ​Agei,t−1\Delta\mathrm{Age}_{i,t-1} predicted incident diagnosis in interval tt:

hi​(t)=h0​(t)​exp⁡(βΔ​Δ​Agei,t−1+βA​Agei,0+βB​BMIi,0+𝜷S⊤​𝐒i),h_{i}(t)=h_{0}(t)\exp\left(\beta_{\Delta}\Delta\mathrm{Age}_{i,t-1}+\beta_{A}\mathrm{Age}_{i,0}+\beta_{B}\mathrm{BMI}_{i,0}+\boldsymbol{\beta}_{S}^{\top}\mathbf{S}_{i}\right), (15)

where Agei,0\mathrm{Age}_{i,0} denotes chronological age at baseline, BMIi,0\mathrm{BMI}_{i,0} denotes baseline BMI, and 𝐒i\mathbf{S}_{i} denotes indicator variables for sex. Participant trajectories were represented as start–stop intervals in days since baseline, with the stop time of event windows truncated at the exact diagnosis date. An L2L_{2} ridge penalty of 10−410^{-4} was applied for numerical stability. The lagged time-varying analysis included 13,84213{,}842 participants (164,336164{,}336 intervals; 906906 events); full model estimates are reported in Extended Data Table 2.

4.1.11 Incremental prognostic discrimination (Harrell’s C-index)

To assess whether CHA adds genuine prognostic discrimination beyond routine clinical chart variables, we compared nested baseline Cox proportional hazards models in the disease-free cohort with complete baseline covariates (N=14,663N=14{,}663 participants; 1,4021{,}402 incident composite diagnoses): (1) a Baseline Clinical Model comprising chronological age, sex, and baseline BMI alone, and (2) an extended Baseline + CHA model incorporating baseline Health Age Delta. Model discrimination was quantified using Harrell’s concordance index (C-index). We evaluated the incremental gain in concordance (Δ​C=Cfull−Cbase\Delta C=C_{\mathrm{full}}-C_{\mathrm{base}}) using 500-iteration paired bootstrap resampling to derive 95% confidence intervals and two-sided pp-values, alongside a nested likelihood ratio test (χ2\chi^{2} with 1 degree of freedom). To verify out-of-sample generalizability and rule out overfitting, we computed out-of-sample risk predictions using 5-fold event-stratified cross-validation. Finally, because chronological age alone strongly separates risk across wide age spans, we performed pre-specified age-stratified subgroup evaluations in younger and middle-aged adults (<50<50 years; N=7,399N=7{,}399, 549549 events) and older adults (≥50\geq 50 years; N=7,264N=7{,}264, 853853 events) to test whether CHA improves risk ranking among peers of similar chronological age (Extended Data Table 3).

4.1.12 Detailed clinical reference measures

4.1.12.1 Modified Life’s Essential 8.

The modified Life’s Essential 8 measure was based on the American Heart Association Life’s Essential 8 cardiovascular-health framework Lloyd-Jones et al. (2022). Because standardized dietary-intake data were unavailable, the dietary domain was omitted and the remaining seven cardiovascular-health domains were retained. Each domain was scored from 0 to 100 according to the corresponding Life’s Essential 8 criteria, and the final mod-LE8 score was calculated as

mod​-​LE8=17​∑k=17Sk,\mathrm{mod\mbox{-}LE8}=\frac{1}{7}\sum_{k=1}^{7}S_{k}, (16)

where SkS_{k} denotes the score for each retained cardiovascular-health domain.

Physical activity was calculated from wearable-derived weekly AZM. Participants accumulating at least 150 active minutes per week received 100 points, with lower activity scaled toward zero.

Sleep health was calculated from mean wearable-measured main-sleep duration. Sleep durations between 7 and 9 hours received 100 points. Very short sleep (<4<4 hours) or very long sleep (>10>10 hours) received zero points, with intermediate durations scored according to the corresponding cardiovascular-health scoring scheme.

Nicotine exposure was derived from self-report. Current nicotine use or regular environmental exposure received zero points, whereas participants without reported exposure received 100 points.

BMI was calculated from clinical height and weight measurements. BMI below 25 kg m-2 received 100 points, with progressively lower scores at higher BMI and zero points at BMI ≥40\geq 40 kg m-2.

Blood pressure scoring used clinical systolic and diastolic blood-pressure measurements and antihypertensive-treatment status. Untreated blood pressure below 120/80 mmHg received 100 points. Blood pressure controlled through antihypertensive treatment was capped at 80 points.

Blood-lipid scoring used non-HDL cholesterol and lipid-lowering-treatment status. Untreated non-HDL cholesterol below 130 mg/dL received 100 points, while scores for participants receiving lipid-lowering therapy were capped at 80 points.

Blood-glucose scoring was based on HbA1c together with diabetes history. Among participants without diabetes, HbA1c below 5.7% received 100 points. Among participants with diabetes, scoring reflected degree of glycaemic control, with well-controlled diabetes (HbA1c <7.0%<7.0\%) receiving at most 40 points and poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c >9.0%>9.0\%) receiving 10 points.

4.1.12.2 Metabolic Syndrome Severity Score.

MSSS was calculated according to the continuous confirmatory-factor-analysis framework developed for Metabolic Syndrome Severity Gurka et al. (2014). The score incorporates BMI, systolic blood pressure, fasting plasma glucose, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol. Scores were standardized as zz-scores within sex and race/ethnicity strata, including Non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, and Non-Hispanic White/general strata. Positive scores represent metabolic severity above the corresponding U.S. adult reference distribution. Only participants with complete measurements for all five components were included.

4.1.13 Comparator age formulations

4.1.13.1 Phenotypic Age.

Phenotypic Age (PhenoAge) was calculated according to the multi-system mortality-risk formulation developed by Levine et al. Levine et al. (2018). The formulation uses chronological age and nine clinical biomarkers: albumin, creatinine, glucose, C-reactive protein, lymphocyte percentage, mean cell volume, red-cell distribution width, alkaline phosphatase, and white-blood-cell count. Participants missing any required variable were excluded.

The linear predictor was

x​b=\displaystyle xb=\; −19.907−0.0336​Albumin+0.0095​Creatinine+0.1953​Glucose\displaystyle-19.907-0.0336\,\mathrm{Albumin}+0.0095\,\mathrm{Creatinine}+0.1953\,\mathrm{Glucose}
+0.0954​log⁡(CRP)−0.0120​Lymphocyte+0.0268​MCV+0.3306​RDW\displaystyle+0.0954\log(\mathrm{CRP})-0.0120\,\mathrm{Lymphocyte}+0.0268\,\mathrm{MCV}+0.3306\,\mathrm{RDW}
+0.0019​ALP+0.0554​WBC+0.0804​Age.\displaystyle+0.0019\,\mathrm{ALP}+0.0554\,\mathrm{WBC}+0.0804\,\mathrm{Age}. (17)

The corresponding cumulative hazard was

H⁡(t)=exp⁡(x​b)​[exp⁡(γ​t)−1]γ,t=120,γ=0.0076927,H(t)=\frac{\exp(xb)\left[\exp(\gamma t)-1\right]}{\gamma},\hskip 20.00003ptt=120,\hskip 20.00003pt\gamma=0.0076927, (18)

with 10-year mortality probability

M=1−exp⁡[−H⁡(t)].M=1-\exp[-H(t)]. (19)

This probability was transformed to a clinical Phenotypic Age,

ClinicalPhenoAge=141.50225+log⁡[−0.00553​log⁡(1−M)]0.090165,\mathrm{ClinicalPhenoAge}=141.50225+\frac{\log[-0.00553\log(1-M)]}{0.090165}, (20)

followed by the scaling transformation used in the analysis,

PhenoAge=ClinicalPhenoAge1+1.28047​exp⁡[0.0344329​(ClinicalPhenoAge−182.344)].\mathrm{PhenoAge}=\frac{\mathrm{ClinicalPhenoAge}}{1+1.28047\exp[0.0344329(\mathrm{ClinicalPhenoAge}-182.344)]}. (21)
4.1.13.2 Wearable chronological-age model.

As a wearable-based chronological-age comparator, daily multimodal wearable measurements were encoded using the pretrained Sensor Foundation Model (SensorFM) Narayanswamy et al. (2026). Participants were required to have at least 14 valid wearable days. Daily embeddings were median-pooled across valid days to obtain one participant-level embedding.

Embeddings were standardized to zero mean and unit variance and reduced using principal component analysis. The minimum number of principal components explaining at least 95% of cumulative variance was retained. An XGBoost regressor was then trained to predict chronological age using five-fold cross-validation. Hyperparameters, including L1 and L2 regularization, row and column subsampling, and tree depth, were selected within the training folds. Out-of-fold predictions were retained for evaluation.

Chronological-age prediction from physiological measurements can exhibit age-dependent estimation bias resulting from regression toward the mean Smith et al. (2019). We therefore fitted a linear correction between chronological age and the raw age residual. Let

Δraw=Agechrono−Agepred,raw.\Delta_{\mathrm{raw}}=\mathrm{Age}_{\mathrm{chrono}}-\mathrm{Age}_{\mathrm{pred,raw}}. (22)

We fitted

Bias⁡(Agechrono)=α​Agechrono+β,\mathrm{Bias}(\mathrm{Age}_{\mathrm{chrono}})=\alpha\mathrm{Age}_{\mathrm{chrono}}+\beta, (23)

and calculated

Δunbiased=Δraw−Bias⁡(Agechrono).\Delta_{\mathrm{unbiased}}=\Delta_{\mathrm{raw}}-\mathrm{Bias}(\mathrm{Age}_{\mathrm{chrono}}). (24)

The bias-adjusted wearable age was then

Agewearable=Agechrono−Δunbiased.\mathrm{Age}_{\mathrm{wearable}}=\mathrm{Age}_{\mathrm{chrono}}-\Delta_{\mathrm{unbiased}}. (25)
4.1.13.3 Exploratory LLM-derived Health Age.

We additionally evaluated an exploratory LLM-derived Health Age estimate using gemini-3.1-pro-preview. Two wearable-input configurations were considered. The first contained multi-day WEAR-ME measurements including blood-oxygen saturation, sleep score, AZM, sleep duration, steps, and heart-rate variability. The second contained the same curated measurements used by CHA. The model was instructed to return a single integer representing estimated health age.

Generation was evaluated at temperatures T∈{0.1,0.5,1.0}T\in\{0.1,0.5,1.0\}, with three independent generations per participant and temperature. Server-side caching was disabled. Within-temperature reliability was quantified using the average participant-level standard deviation, ICC(3,1), and ICC(3,kk) with k=3k=3.

Across-temperature sensitivity was assessed among participants with complete estimates at all three temperatures. Mean estimates across the three replicates were compared using the Friedman test. When the omnibus test was significant, pairwise comparisons were conducted with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Bonferroni correction across the three temperature comparisons.

4.2 Trajectory prediction with SensorWM

4.2.1 Pretraining data and longitudinal wearable representation

World models learn transition functions that describe how an observed system evolves over time and can be recursively applied to generate future state trajectories Ha and Schmidhuber (2018); LeCun and others (2022); Ding et al. (2025). We adapted this formulation to longitudinal wearable data by representing each participant as a sequence of physiological states and observable behavioral actions and learning how physiological state evolves as a function of both recent trajectory and behavioral context.

SensorWM was developed using a large longitudinal dataset of naturalistic wearable measurements collected during routine Fitbit use. The pretraining cohort contained 96,957 participants (2.28 million total person-weeks; 182,797 valid 12-week windows). Participants contributing to the pretraining dataset provided informed consent authorizing use of de-identified data for research and health-and-wellness product development. Data collection and analysis were conducted under centralized institutional review board protocol WCG 20253840. Demographic and longitudinal characteristics of the pretraining population are reported in Table 1.

Wearable measurements spanned cardiovascular, cardiopulmonary, sleep, skin-temperature, physical-activity, and physiological-variability domains. We partitioned these measurements into physiological state variables and behavioral action variables. State variables represented the participant’s observed physiological condition and included resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, respiratory rate, blood-oxygen saturation, sleep architecture, skin temperature, heart-rate-zone measurements, and longitudinal variability features. Demographic characteristics were included as static state information. Three directly observable behaviors were designated as actions: daily step count, main-sleep duration, and cardio-intensity minutes. The complete feature inventory and state–action assignments are reported in Supplementary Table 6.

Wearable measurements were harmonized to a weekly temporal resolution. Weekly representations provide a compromise between short-timescale sensor variability and the loss of temporal information associated with much coarser aggregation, and are consistent with previous approaches for representing longitudinal event streams and repeated health measurements McDermott et al. (2023); Lee et al. (2025); McDermott et al. (2026). This timescale also corresponds to the timescale over which many sleep and physical-activity exposures are commonly summarized Atkinson and Davenne (2007); Buysse et al. (2010); Powell et al. (2011).

Continuous physiological measurements, behavioral and count-based measurements were aggregated over available observation days and normalized by the number of valid days. For feature xx observed on the set of valid days 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} during week tt, the weekly aggregate was

xtweek=∑d∈𝒟txd|𝒟t|.x_{t}^{\mathrm{week}}=\frac{\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}_{t}}x_{d}}{|\mathcal{D}_{t}|}. (26)

This normalization prevented incomplete device wear from being interpreted mechanically as reduced activity or physiological function. Continuous features were standardized using the corresponding mean and standard deviation estimated from the pretraining data,

x~=x−μtrainσtrain.\widetilde{x}=\frac{x-\mu_{\mathrm{train}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{train}}}. (27)

Each participant was subsequently represented as a longitudinal state–action sequence

(s1,a1,s2,a2,…,sT,aT),T≤24,(s_{1},a_{1},s_{2},a_{2},\ldots,s_{T},a_{T}),\hskip 20.00003ptT\leq 24, (28)

where sts_{t} denotes the physiological state during week tt and ata_{t} denotes the corresponding behavioral action vector.

4.2.2 WEAR-ME evaluation cohort

SensorWM was evaluated in an independent subset of 1,654 participants from the WEAR-ME study who contained classification labels Metwally et al. (2026); this subset was defined by the availability of longitudinal wearable measurements alongside clinical, behavioral, medication, or laboratory-derived labels, which were not present for all 2,780 cohort participants. Evaluation participants were held out from world-model pretraining. Participants contributed an average of 19.6±4.219.6\pm 4.2 weeks (0.38±0.080.38\pm 0.08 years; up to 24 weeks) of wearable observations, providing longitudinal context for evaluating whether SensorWM preserved physiologically meaningful temporal information.

The evaluation benchmark included diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, kidney disease, respiratory disease, HOMA-IR defined insulin resistance, smoking status, menstrual regularity, and cardiovascular, diabetes, thyroid, mental-health, and general medication-use outcomes. Labels originated from participant questionnaires, medication records, or laboratory measurements depending on the task. All training, validation, and test partitions were defined at the participant level to prevent observations from the same individual appearing across data splits. Complete task definitions, sample sizes, outcome prevalence, demographic characteristics, longitudinal coverage, and task-specific split statistics are reported in Supplementary Tables 7, 9, and 10.

State–action feature specification

The complete set of state and action variables supplied to SensorWM is reported in Supplementary Table 6. The feature representation combined measurements across demographic, cardiovascular, cardiopulmonary, sleep, skin-surface, motion, and regularity or variability domains. Longitudinal wearable and event-stream representations spanning multiple physiological domains have similarly been used to capture temporally evolving health information in prior work McDermott et al. (2023); Lee et al. (2025); McDermott et al. (2026).

Only step count, main-sleep asleep minutes, and cardio-intensity minutes were designated as behavioral actions. All remaining wearable measurements were treated as state variables, including physiological responses associated with behaviour, such as heart-rate-zone occupancy. Demographic variables were treated as static contextual state information.

This operational distinction was maintained during both pretraining and alternative-behaviour rollout. Action variables could be externally replaced by prespecified future sequences, whereas state variables were generated through the learned physiological dynamics. The state–action terminology denotes the role of a variable in SensorWM and does not imply that observational associations between actions and subsequent states identify causal intervention effects.

Temporal aggregation and preprocessing

The underlying Fitbit measurements were available at heterogeneous temporal resolutions ranging from minute-level physiological streams to daily summary measurements. Directly modeling transitions at the highest available sampling frequency would emphasize substantial short-timescale variation and increase sequence length, whereas very coarse aggregation would reduce the number of available longitudinal transitions. We therefore represented the wearable data on a common weekly grid. Similar temporal harmonization is commonly used for longitudinal health-event representations McDermott et al. (2023); Lee et al. (2025); McDermott et al. (2026), and weekly summaries correspond naturally to established reporting intervals for sleep and physical activity Atkinson and Davenne (2007); Buysse et al. (2010); Powell et al. (2011).

Continuous physiological variables, including heart-rate variability, respiratory rate, blood-oxygen saturation, and temperature-related measurements, were summarized within each weekly interval. Behavioral and count-based variables were aggregated over valid observation days and normalized by the number of observed days according to Eq. 26. Continuous variables were subsequently standardized using pretraining-set statistics according to Eq. 27. The same stored normalization parameters were used during downstream inference and to invert decoded predictions to their original physiological units.

4.2.3 Action-conditioned latent dynamics

SensorWM was adapted from joint-embedding predictive approaches in which an encoder and latent transition model are optimized jointly without requiring reconstruction of the original observations LeCun and others (2022); Maes et al. (2026). Let

st∈ℝns,at∈ℝna,s_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{s}},\hskip 20.00003pta_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{a}}, (29)

denote the physiological state and behavioral action vector, respectively, during week tt. A state encoder EE maps the physiological state to a d=128d=128 dimensional latent representation,

zt=E⁡(st),zt∈ℝ128.z_{t}=E(s_{t}),\hskip 20.00003ptz_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{128}. (30)

SensorWM models second-order dynamics in latent physiological space,

p⁡(zt+1∣zt,zt−1,at).p(z_{t+1}\mid z_{t},z_{t-1},a_{t}). (31)

Equivalently, the process can be represented as first-order Markov in an augmented state containing the current latent representation and its recent displacement,

Δ​zt=zt−zt−1.\Delta z_{t}=z_{t}-z_{t-1}. (32)

The inclusion of Δ​zt\Delta z_{t} allows the model to distinguish participants occupying similar current physiological states but moving through latent space in different directions.

The encoder was implemented as a multilayer perceptron with hidden dimension 256 and latent dimension 128, using batch normalization, ReLU nonlinearities, and dropout. This latent dimensionality provides sufficient capacity for multivariate temporal representations while limiting the dimensionality of the learned transition space Wang et al. (2026).

The latent transition model was parameterized by a predictor network gg. Given the current latent state and behavioral action, the predictor generated a state-dependent linear transition operator,

Ft=g⁡(zt,at),Ft∈ℝ128×128.F_{t}=g(z_{t},a_{t}),\hskip 20.00003ptF_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{128\times 128}. (33)

Thus, SensorWM does not learn a single global linear dynamical system. Instead, the transition operator varies as a function of the participant’s current physiological representation and behavioral context.

Behavioral information was incorporated into the predictor using adaptive layer normalization and a multiplicative action gate following the action-conditioning formulation used in LeWorldModel Maes et al. (2026). The action-conditioning scale and shift parameters were initialized at zero, such that optimization began near an unconditioned transition model and action dependence was learned progressively. Spectral normalization was applied to linear layers of the predictor to constrain the magnitude of the transition mapping during recursive rollout.

Rather than predicting each future latent state independently, SensorWM transforms the participant’s preceding latent displacement. The predicted displacement is

Δ​z^t+1=Ft​Δ​zt,\widehat{\Delta z}_{t+1}=F_{t}\Delta z_{t}, (34)

and the subsequent latent state is obtained by discrete integration,

z^t+1=zt+Δ​z^t+1.\widehat{z}_{t+1}=z_{t}+\widehat{\Delta z}_{t+1}. (35)

Combining Eqs. 32–35,

z^t+1=zt+g⁡(zt,at)​(zt−zt−1).\widehat{z}_{t+1}=z_{t}+g(z_{t},a_{t})\left(z_{t}-z_{t-1}\right). (36)

This parameterization represents physiological evolution as an action-dependent transformation of the participant’s recent direction of movement through latent space. The learned operator can preserve, attenuate, amplify, or rotate the previous displacement according to the current physiological state and supplied behavior.

Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization

SensorWM used Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg), following the representation regularization used in LeWorldModel Maes et al. (2026), to discourage collapse of the jointly learned latent representation. The target aggregate latent distribution was an isotropic standard Gaussian,

z∼𝒩⁡(0,I).z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (37)

Rather than estimating the full high-dimensional distribution directly, SIGReg projected minibatch latent representations onto randomly sampled one-dimensional directions and quantified deviation from a standard Gaussian using an Epps–Pulley characteristic-function criterion. Each regularization step used 256 random projections.

SIGReg was applied jointly with the rollout and trajectory-path objectives described in the main Methods. It therefore provided an anti-collapse constraint without requiring an input-reconstruction objective, explicit contrastive negative examples, a momentum-updated target encoder, or stop-gradient target representations.

4.2.4 Multi-step trajectory training

SensorWM was trained using 12-week longitudinal rollout windows. Each trajectory was initialized from the first two observed physiological states,

z^0=z0∗=E⁡(s0),z^1=z1∗=E⁡(s1),\widehat{z}_{0}=z_{0}^{*}=E(s_{0}),\hskip 20.00003pt\widehat{z}_{1}=z_{1}^{*}=E(s_{1}), (38)

with initial latent displacement

Δ​z^1=z1∗−z0∗.\widehat{\Delta z}_{1}=z_{1}^{*}-z_{0}^{*}. (39)

Subsequent states were generated recursively. At rollout step tt,

F^t\displaystyle\widehat{F}_{t} =g⁡(z^t,at),\displaystyle=g(\widehat{z}_{t},a_{t}), (40)
Δ​z^t+1\displaystyle\widehat{\Delta z}_{t+1} =F^t​Δ​z^t,\displaystyle=\widehat{F}_{t}\widehat{\Delta z}_{t}, (41)
z^t+1\displaystyle\widehat{z}_{t+1} =z^t+Δ​z^t+1.\displaystyle=\widehat{z}_{t}+\widehat{\Delta z}_{t+1}. (42)

After initialization, predicted states rather than future observed states were supplied to subsequent transitions. Prediction errors at earlier rollout steps could therefore propagate to later steps during training, exposing the model to the same recursive dynamics subsequently used during inference.

For each future week, the latent target was produced by applying the jointly trained encoder to the observed physiological state,

zt+1∗=E⁡(st+1).z_{t+1}^{*}=E(s_{t+1}). (43)

The primary rollout objective was

ℒroll=1|ℳ|​∑t∈ℳ‖z^t+1−zt+1∗‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}}\left\|\widehat{z}_{t+1}-z_{t+1}^{*}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (44)

where ℳ\mathcal{M} denotes the set of valid transitions in the training window.

We additionally constrained the local direction of the learned trajectory. The empirical displacement between consecutively encoded observed states was

Δ​zt+1∗=zt+1∗−zt∗,\Delta z_{t+1}^{*}=z_{t+1}^{*}-z_{t}^{*}, (45)

and the trajectory-path objective was

ℒpath=1|ℳ|​∑t∈ℳ‖Δ​z^t+1−Δ​zt+1∗‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{path}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{M}}\left\|\widehat{\Delta z}_{t+1}-\Delta z_{t+1}^{*}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (46)

The rollout and path objectives therefore constrain complementary properties of the learned dynamics: ℒroll\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}} penalizes errors in the predicted latent location, whereas ℒpath\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{path}} penalizes errors in the direction and magnitude of local movement. The complete SensorWM training objective was

ℒSensorWM=λMSE​ℒroll+λpath​ℒpath+λSIG​ℒSIG,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SensorWM}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{MSE}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{roll}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{path}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{path}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{SIG}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIG}}, (47)

with λMSE=1\lambda_{\mathrm{MSE}}=1. During model development, λpath\lambda_{\mathrm{path}} was evaluated over the range 1.5–3.0 dynamically adjusted during pre-training and λSIG=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{SIG}}=0.1. The implementation of SIGReg is described in Methods 4.2.

The encoder and transition predictor were optimized jointly using AdamW with an initial learning rate of 3×10−53\times 10^{-5} and weight decay of 10−310^{-3}. Global gradient norm was clipped at 1.0.

4.2.5 Diagnostic physiological decoder and recursive forecasting

SensorWM pretraining was performed entirely in latent space and did not require reconstruction of the original wearable measurements, consistent with the joint-embedding predictive formulation on which the architecture was based LeCun and others (2022); Maes et al. (2026). To evaluate predicted trajectories in physiological units, we subsequently trained a post hoc linear decoder DD,

s^t=D⁡(zt),\widehat{s}_{t}=D(z_{t}), (48)

while keeping the pretrained encoder and transition predictor fixed. The decoder was optimized using masked mean-squared error such that only observed physiological measurements contributed to the loss. AdamW was used with learning rate 10−310^{-3} and weight decay 10−410^{-4}. Fifteen percent of decoder-training observations were reserved for internal validation. Training used early stopping, and the parameters corresponding to the lowest validation loss were restored before evaluation. The decoder did not contribute gradients to the encoder or transition predictor and therefore did not alter the pretrained SensorWM representation.

For action-conditioned forecasting, each participant was initialized from the two most recent observed physiological states,

z0=E⁡(s0),z1=E⁡(s1),Δ​z1=z1−z0.z_{0}=E(s_{0}),\hskip 20.00003ptz_{1}=E(s_{1}),\hskip 20.00003pt\Delta z_{1}=z_{1}-z_{0}. (49)

SensorWM was then propagated autoregressively using the participant’s recorded behavioral action sequence over the forecasting horizon. At each prediction step, the corresponding behavioral action vector was supplied as an exogenous input to condition the physiological transition. Future physiological states were predicted recursively without access to future observed physiological measurements.

Ft\displaystyle F_{t} =g⁡(zt,at),\displaystyle=g(z_{t},a_{t}), (50)
Δ​zt+1\displaystyle\Delta z_{t+1} =Ft​Δ​zt,\displaystyle=F_{t}\Delta z_{t}, (51)
zt+1\displaystyle z_{t+1} =zt+Δ​zt+1.\displaystyle=z_{t}+\Delta z_{t+1}. (52)

No future physiological measurements were provided after rollout initialization. Subsequent physiological states were predicted autoregressively using the action-conditioned latent transition dynamics defined in Eq. 52.

Feature-level forecasting performance was quantified using the coefficient of determination (R2R^{2}) and Pearson correlation coefficient over the population. SensorWM was compared with the mean of the preceding one, two, and four weeks, last observation carried forward (LOCF), and TimesFM Das et al. (2024) as a general-purpose time-series forecasting model.

Complete feature-level R2R^{2} and correlation results are reported in Supplementary Tables 11–12.

4.2.6 Trajectory and downstream information fidelity

We evaluated whether SensorWM-generated trajectories preserved both the geometric structure and clinically relevant information contained in observed longitudinal wearable measurements.

To visualize trajectory geometry, observed wearable sequences were passed through the frozen SensorWM encoder to obtain 128-dimensional latent representations at each weekly time point and compared against the generated latent features. Principal-component analysis was fitted to the combined set of observed and generated latent states, and the same transformation was applied to both. The first two principal components were used to visualize participant-specific trajectories, enabling direct comparison of their direction, dispersion, and temporal evolution in a common coordinate system.

We next evaluated whether generated trajectories retained information relevant to downstream health prediction. For each task, the observed longitudinal Fitbit sequence and corresponding SensorWM-generated trajectory were evaluated using matched gated recurrent unit (GRU) sequence classifiers Chung et al. (2014). The classifier architecture, optimization procedure, train–validation–test partition, and outcome definition were held fixed between observed and generated inputs so that performance differences reflected information retained by the generated trajectory rather than differences in downstream model capacity.

We additionally compared the trajectory-based representations with two non-trajectory baselines derived from the same wearable data: features obtained from the first week of wearable observations and embeddings generated by the pretrained SensorFM Narayanswamy et al. (2026). Representations were mapped to a common 128-dimensional space for controlled comparison. The observed and SensorWM-generated longitudinal sequences were evaluated with the same GRU-based sequence-classification framework Chung et al. (2014), whereas the comparison representations supplied static participant-level information.

Classification performance was quantified using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). For the primary comparison between observed and SensorWM-generated trajectories, differences in paired AUROCs were assessed using DeLong’s test DeLong et al. (1988) for correlated receiver operating characteristic curves.

Failure to reject the null hypothesis was interpreted as an absence of a detectable difference rather than as formal statistical equivalence. Complete classification results and additional robustness analyses are reported in Supplementary Tables 15–24 and Supplementary Results A.

4.2.7 Alternative-behavior rollouts

The same frozen transition model was subsequently evaluated under prespecified alternative behavioral sequences. For each participant, the physiological initialization was held fixed while the recorded future action sequence {at}t=1K\{a_{t}\}_{t=1}^{K} was replaced with an alternative sequence {a~t}t=1K\{\widetilde{a}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{K}. SensorWM was then propagated autoregressively using the behavioral action vector at each forecast step. Specifically, the transition operator was conditioned on the current predicted latent physiological state and the corresponding action vector, and was applied to the preceding latent state difference to predict the subsequent physiological state.

z~t+1=z~t+g⁡(z~t,a~t)​(z~t−z~t−1),\widetilde{z}_{t+1}=\widetilde{z}_{t}+g(\widetilde{z}_{t},\widetilde{a}_{t})\left(\widetilde{z}_{t}-\widetilde{z}_{t-1}\right), (53)

and decoded to physiological space as

s~t=D⁡(z~t).\widetilde{s}_{t}=D(\widetilde{z}_{t}). (54)

Observed-action and alternative-action trajectories therefore shared the same initial physiological history and differed in the behavioral sequence supplied to the learned transition model. Their divergence represents a model-implied conditional difference under the specified action sequences. Because SensorWM was trained using observational wearable data, these alternative trajectories were interpreted as conditional model projections rather than identified causal effects of behavioral intervention.

4.3 Agentic Counterfactual Coaching

4.3.1 WEAR-ME cohort and feature preprocessing

Participants for the coaching evaluations were drawn from the WEAR-ME study (N=2,780N=2{,}780 participants with complete demographic linkage and at least three valid weeks of longitudinal wearable data). Inputs to plan generation comprised wearable-derived baseline metrics, chronological age, CHA, resting heart rate (RHR), daily steps, device-measured sleep duration, Active Zone Minutes (AZM), and cardiorespiratory fitness, together with each participant’s habitual distributions (up to 24 weeks; mean 19.6±4.219.6\pm 4.2 weeks, corresponding to 0.38±0.080.38\pm 0.08 years and 3,289 complete 12-week windows in Table 1), historical peaks, and model-projected trajectories. All data were de-identified and accessed under the study’s institutional governance and privacy controls.

Per-domain daily wearable records were aggregated to ISO calendar weeks by computing the weekly mean of daily values, yielding one weekly feature vector per participant. Static features were harmonized to standard units (weight in kilograms, height in meters, body mass index [BMI] in kg/m2\text{kg/m}^{2}), and chronological age was derived from birth year. Each feature was standardized to zero mean and unit variance using pre-trained cohort-level statistics. Features were partitioned into participant-controllable actions (volitional behaviors: daily steps, main-sleep duration in minutes, and cardiorespiratory exercise minutes) and observed physiological states (RHR, AZM, and remaining physiological markers). Sequences were padded to a uniform length with an accompanying validity mask.

4.3.2 Counterfactual simulation and feasibility-constrained optimization

For each participant, we simulated a set of feasible 12-week behavior-change scenarios and their projected physiological consequences, casting plan selection as a constrained optimization problem that trades projected CHA improvement against individualized behavioral effort.

Candidate space and counterfactual rollouts.

By construction, candidate 0 (all targets equal to baseline) represents the “do-nothing” scenario, in which observed behavioral levels are held constant over the 12-week forecasting horizon. Its projected endpoint defines the status-quo anchor, CHAsq\mathrm{CHA}_{\text{sq}}. For each intervention candidate cc, we defined the projected counterfactual benefit as Δ​CHA​(c)=CHAsq−CHAc\Delta\mathrm{CHA}(c)=\mathrm{CHA}_{\text{sq}}-\mathrm{CHA}_{c}, where CHAc\mathrm{CHA}_{c} denotes the corresponding 12-week projected CHA. This future-versus-future comparison measures the incremental benefit of behavioral modification relative to continued habitual behavior, rather than the absolute change from the participant’s observed baseline CHA, thereby accounting for physiological drift predicted under unchanged actions.

Personalized effort and optimization objective.

To reflect individual behavioral flexibility rather than population-average difficulty, we estimated per-action variability σkuser\sigma^{\text{user}}_{k} as the within-participant standard deviation of action kk over the participant’s historical wearable record, bounded below by safety floors (500 steps, 15 sleep minutes, and 10 cardiorespiratory exercise minutes) so that highly consistent participants were not assigned near-infinite effort penalties. Personalized effort was defined as the sum of squared, self-standardized deviations from baseline:

E⁡(c)=∑k∈{step,sleep,cardio}(ck−bkσkuser)2.E(c)\;=\;\sum_{k\in\{\text{step},\,\text{sleep},\,\text{cardio}\}}\left(\frac{c_{k}-b_{k}}{\sigma^{\text{user}}_{k}}\right)^{\!2}. (55)

Each candidate trajectory was scored by its projected CHA reduction per unit of personalized effort,

score⁡(c)=Δ​CHA​(c)1+E⁡(c)=CHAsq−CHAc1+E⁡(c),\mathrm{score}(c)\;=\;\frac{\Delta\mathrm{CHA}(c)}{1+E(c)}\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{CHA}_{\text{sq}}-\mathrm{CHA}_{c}}{1+E(c)}, (56)

where the additive constant regularizes the ratio at E⁡(c)=0E(c)=0. We discarded candidates whose projected reduction did not exceed a minimal clinically meaningful threshold (CHAsq−CHAc>0.1​ years\mathrm{CHA}_{\text{sq}}-\mathrm{CHA}_{c}>0.1\text{ years}) and ranked the remaining feasible trajectories by Eq. (56). The ranked candidates were subsequently organized into three behavioral pathways corresponding to sleep-focused, movement-focused, and combined interventions. Up to three pathways were provided to the coaching agent as Option 1, Option 2, and Option 3, together with the status-quo projection CHAsq\mathrm{CHA}_{\text{sq}}, participant-specific historical wearable ranges, and recorded behavioral peaks. Each option described the proposed behavioral targets and their projected 12-week changes in CHA and resting heart rate, allowing the agent to synthesize a personalized coaching plan from distinct behavioral alternatives. Sensitivity analyses across objective hyperparameters are reported in the Supplementary Information.

Action–outcome firewall.

The optimization exposes only volitional behavioral actions (steps, sleep duration, cardiorespiratory exercise) as recommendable targets; projected physiological states (RHR, AZM, and CHA) are treated strictly as downstream model outcomes and are never prescribed as direct behavioral goals. This separation is enforced in the generation prompt and audited in evaluation, preventing the agent from instructing a user to “lower your resting heart rate” rather than prescribing the behavioral modifications projected to achieve that outcome.

4.3.3 Paired coaching-plan generation and two-arm study design

To isolate the contribution of CHA and SensorWM counterfactual projections, we used a two-arm, within-participant paired design. For each participant, two 12-week personalized lifestyle coaching plans were generated from identical baseline demographic and longitudinal wearable histories (up to 24 weeks; recent daily averages, habitual means, standard deviations, minimum–maximum ranges, and historical peaks) using the same underlying language model (gemini-3.5-flash, temperature 0.20.2, served via the OneTwo interface):

  • •

    Generic Coaching Arm (Baseline Control): Conditioned on the participant’s demographics, baseline wearable metrics, 24-week habitual distributions, and historical peaks, but without access to CHA or SensorWM counterfactual simulations. The model was instructed to synthesize the wearable history and construct a progressive 12-week behavior-change plan across three 4-week phases (Weeks 1–4: Foundation, Weeks 5–8: Build, and Weeks 9–12: Sustain).

  • •

    Counterfactual Coaching Arm (Full System): Conditioned on the identical demographic and longitudinal wearable context plus the participant’s baseline CHA, the 12-week status-quo projection (Future A: If No Habit Changes, CHAsq\mathrm{CHA}_{\text{sq}}), and the top feasibility-ranked counterfactual pathways (Future B: Your Counterfactual Options), quantifying projected changes in CHA (Δ​CHA\Delta\text{CHA}), RHR (Δ​RHR\Delta\text{RHR}), and AZM alongside historical-best self-efficacy anchors.

To prevent confounding from stylistic or structural formatting differences, both arms were governed by strict Universal Tone and Formatting Parity Guardrails (Supplementary Information C.3), enforcing an identical 500–700-word target length, an identical four-part layout (Your Health Snapshot, 12-Week Progressive Plan, Evidence-Based Habit Formation, and Summary), explicit Self-Determination Theory (SDT) motivational interviewing principles (implementation intentions, coping planning, self-monitoring, and autonomy support), and a prohibition against clinical jargon or fear/shame-based framing. All plan generation and evaluations were conducted offline using retrospective participant profiles.

Experimental Prompt Architectures and Universal Tone Parity Guardrails

To ensure a rigorous scientific comparison between the Generic Coaching Arm and the Counterfactual Coaching Arm, both prompts were engineered under strict Tone, Structure, and Length Parity Guardrails. In preliminary pilot testing, unaligned baseline prompts tended to produce dry, bulleted clinical summaries, whereas counterfactual prompts produced warm, narrative coaching, confounding the informational value of counterfactual simulations with stylistic warmth. We eliminated this confounder by enforcing identical persona instructions, identical Self-Determination Theory (SDT) motivational interviewing principles, identical formatting constraints, and an identical four-section output schema across both arms:

  1. 1.

    Tone & Empathy: Warm, supportive, non-judgmental, collaborative, and empowering; strict prohibition against fear-based, alarmist, or shame-inducing language.

  2. 2.

    No Clinical or Statistical Jargon: Explicit ban on raw statistical or variable tokens (such as std, min/max, wearable_rhr, counterfactual, baseline delta, or intervention vector). All physiological concepts (such as Resting Heart Rate and Active Zone Minutes) must be explained in accessible, everyday language.

  3. 3.

    Target Length Parity: Strictly bounded to 500–700 words across both arms so raters could not distinguish arms by verbosity.

  4. 4.

    Four-Section Structural Parity:

    • •

      Section 1: YOUR HEALTH SNAPSHOT (Generic) / YOUR HEALTH SNAPSHOT & HEALTH AGE (Counterfactual).

    • •

      Section 2: YOUR 12-WEEK PROGRESSIVE PLAN (Generic) / YOUR COUNTERFACTUAL PATHS & 12-WEEK PLAN (Counterfactual), structured identically into Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4: Foundation), Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8: Build), and Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12: Sustain).

    • •

      Section 3: EVIDENCE-BASED HABIT FORMATION (incorporating habit stacking, implementation intentions, self-monitoring, and barrier troubleshooting).

    • •

      Section 4: SUMMARY & NEXT STEPS (closing with an empowering one-sentence takeaway).

4.3.4 Dual-track human expert evaluation and cohort stratification

Persona stratification and sampling.

To evaluate clinical safety, behavioral quality, and anticipated adherence across diverse user profiles without over-representing median wearable users, we partitioned the WEAR-ME cohort into five prespecified Coachable Personas defined by baseline daily steps, sleep duration, BMI, and Δ​CHA\Delta\text{CHA} (CHA−chronological age\text{CHA}-\text{chronological age}, where CHA denotes the formulation unadjusted for multicollinearity):

  1. 1.

    Persona 1 — Optimal Baseline: High physical activity (≥10,000​ steps/day\geq 10{,}000\text{ steps/day}; sub-cohort mean 13,775​ steps/day13{,}775\text{ steps/day}), adequate sleep (7​–​9​ h/night7\text{--}9\text{ h/night}; mean 7.42​ h7.42\text{ h}), healthy BMI (18.5​–​24.9​ kg/m218.5\text{--}24.9\text{ kg/m}^{2}; mean 22.9​ kg/m222.9\text{ kg/m}^{2}), and favorable Δ​CHA<−1.0​ year\Delta\text{CHA}<-1.0\text{ year} (mean −4.99​ years-4.99\text{ years}; n=78n=78, 2.81%2.81\% of cohort), testing maintenance coaching and ceiling effects.

  2. 2.

    Persona 2 — Multi-Risk Challenger: Sedentary activity (<5,000​ steps/day<5{,}000\text{ steps/day}; mean 3,341​ steps/day3{,}341\text{ steps/day}), insufficient sleep (<7.0​ h/night<7.0\text{ h/night}; mean 6.03​ h6.03\text{ h}), elevated BMI (≥25.0​ kg/m2\geq 25.0\text{ kg/m}^{2}; mean 36.3​ kg/m236.3\text{ kg/m}^{2}), and accelerated Δ​CHA≥+1.0​ year\Delta\text{CHA}\geq+1.0\text{ year} (mean +3.06​ years+3.06\text{ years}; n=277n=277, 9.96%9.96\% of cohort), testing multi-lever prioritization and psychological feasibility.

  3. 3.

    Persona 3 — Recovery Bottleneck: High physical activity (≥10,000​ steps/day\geq 10{,}000\text{ steps/day}; mean 12,738​ steps/day12{,}738\text{ steps/day}) paired with chronic sleep restriction (<7.0​ h/night<7.0\text{ h/night}; mean 6.23​ h6.23\text{ h}; n=354n=354, 12.73%12.73\% of cohort), testing whether the system recognizes activity saturation and isolates sleep and recovery.

  4. 4.

    Persona 4 — Activity Bottleneck: Isolated inactivity (<5,000​ steps/day<5{,}000\text{ steps/day}; mean 3,190​ steps/day3{,}190\text{ steps/day}) with preserved sleep duration (7​–​9​ h/night7\text{--}9\text{ h/night}; mean 7.67​ h7.67\text{ h}) and accelerated Δ​CHA≥+1.0​ year\Delta\text{CHA}\geq+1.0\text{ year} (mean +2.78​ years+2.78\text{ years}; n=227n=227, 8.17%8.17\% of cohort), testing targeted physical activity escalation.

  5. 5.

    Persona 5 — Balanced Maintainer: Moderate daily movement (5,000​–​10,000​ steps/day5{,}000\text{--}10{,}000\text{ steps/day}; mean 5,539​ steps/day5{,}539\text{ steps/day}), adequate sleep (7​–​9​ h/night7\text{--}9\text{ h/night}; mean 7.48​ h7.48\text{ h}), and age-aligned Δ​CHA∈[−1.0,+1.0]​ year\Delta\text{CHA}\in[-1.0,+1.0]\text{ year} (mean −0.31​ years-0.31\text{ years}; n=143n=143, 5.14%5.14\% of cohort), testing progressive habit building in typical users.

Ten participants were randomly sampled from each persona (N=50N=50 cases total). During pre-lock quality control, one case in Persona 5 (Participant ID 57217) was identified as having received identical plan text in both blinded columns due to a serialization collision and was excluded a priori, leaving N=49N=49 valid participant cases (1010 each in Personas 1–4 and 99 in Persona 5; mean chronological age 49.5±6.6​ years49.5\pm 6.6\text{ years}, 57.1%57.1\% female, mean BMI 31.2±7.2​ kg/m231.2\pm 7.2\text{ kg/m}^{2}, mean baseline CHA 53.6±6.1​ years53.6\pm 6.1\text{ years}, Δ​CHA=+4.04±4.52​ years\Delta\text{CHA}=+4.04\pm 4.52\text{ years}). For each case, the Generic and Counterfactual plans were randomly assigned to Plan 1 and Plan 2 via a Bernoulli coin flip (49.0%49.0\% versus 51.0%51.0\%), with all raters blinded to study hypotheses and arm assignments.

Dual-track expert panels and evaluation rubrics.

We convened two complementary panels of domain experts (N=10N=10 raters total):

  1. 1.

    Certified Lifestyle & Health Coaches (n=5n=5): Board-certified health, wellness, and exercise coaches evaluated each plan across 10 behavioral rubric dimensions—comprising 6 binary (Yes/No) dimensions (Easy to Understand, Supportive & Motivating Tone, Trajectory Control, Compelling Reason [No Fear/Shame], Contrasts Benefits vs. Status Quo, and Realistic & Non-Overwhelming) and 4 three-level ordinal dimensions (Signal Synthesis, Baseline & Wearable Personalization, Behavior-Change Strategies, and Sustainable Habit Building)—followed by 2 forced-choice side-by-side (SxS) primary endpoints: Best Overall Coaching Plan and Highest Likelihood of Long-Term Adherence, with mandatory free-text rationale.

  2. 2.

    Board-Certified Clinicians (n=5n=5): Physicians in internal medicine, preventive medicine, and lifestyle/cardiovascular medicine independently audited each plan across 6 clinical dimensions—comprising 5 binary clinical safety and plausibility gates (Safe Intensity Limits, Physiological Claims Correct, 12-Week Biological Plausibility, Trajectory Control, and Contrasts Benefits vs. Status Quo) and 1 three-level ordinal clinical personalization rubric (Baseline & Wearable Personalization).

Three shared dimensions, Contrasts Benefits vs. Status Quo, Trajectory Control, and Baseline & Wearable Personalization, used identical rubric definitions in both expert panels to enable cross-disciplinary concordance analysis. Item-specific denominators are reported in Supplementary Tables 26 and 27 with cross-disciplinary comparisons summarized in Table 28.

4.3.5 Full-cohort automated evaluation with blinded LLM autoraters

To complement the 49-case human expert study and evaluate plan quality across the full eligible WEAR-ME cohort (N=2,780N=2{,}780; n=2,613n=2,613 evaluable paired plans after quality control), we conducted a blinded automated evaluation using a pre-specified, Kirkpatrick-Model inspired four-level rubric Kirkpatrick and others (1959) (Extended Data Table 4). Each of the 12 dimensions across Level 1 (Reaction: Clarity & readability, Tone & motivation, Personal relevance), Level 2 (Learning: Data comprehension, Causal understanding, Insight/stakes), Level 3 (Behavior: Actionability & specificity, Feasibility & progression, Behavior-change technique), and Level 4 (Results: Predicted health impact, Measurability, Evidence grounding) was scored on an anchored 1–5 scale. We computed both an equal-weighted overall score (25%25\% per level) and a priority-weighted overall score (Reaction 0.150.15, Learning 0.300.30, Behavior 0.350.35, Results 0.200.20) Zhang et al. (2026),

overall=∑ℓ=14wℓ​Lℓ,∑ℓ=14wℓ=1,\text{overall}\;=\;\sum_{\ell=1}^{4}w_{\ell}\,L_{\ell},\hskip 20.00003pt\textstyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{4}w_{\ell}=1, (57)

alongside a four-item safety and accuracy gate rating unsafe advice, fabricated numbers, missing medical disclaimer, and factual/physiological error as none, minor, or major (with any major flag capping overall scores at 2.02.0, alongside an uncapped quality index reported separately).

For each participant, the paired Generic and Counterfactual plans were randomly shuffled and relabeled as “Plan 1” and “Plan 2” prior to judging. The autorater received a ground-truth block of the participant’s observed metrics, historical peaks, and model projections, with explicit instructions to evaluate substance rather than length or vocabulary and to treat clearly framed forward-looking projections as legitimate rather than fabricated numbers. Each paired plan set was evaluated three times independently (N=3N=3 passes; primary judge gemini-3.5-flash, temperature 0.50.5), aggregating dimension scores by median, safety flags by worst-case severity, and head-to-head preference by majority vote across passes.

4.3.6 Statistical analysis

All primary comparisons in both the human expert study and the full-cohort automated evaluation used within-participant paired contrasts between the Counterfactual and Generic coaching arms. In the human expert evaluation (N=49N=49 cases; 245 paired evaluations per track, 245 coach evaluations with complete head-to-head responses in Figures 1e and 5), forced-choice head-to-head endpoints (Best Overall Plan and Highest Likelihood of Long-Term Adherence) were tested against the null hypothesis of equal preference (p0=0.50p_{0}=0.50) using two-sided exact binomial tests with Wilson 95%95\% confidence intervals, supplemented by case-level majority consensus (≥3\geq 3 of 55 raters). For per-plan binary and 3-level ordinal rubrics, we prespecified top-box achievement (Yes for binary items; highest anchor for ordinal items) and tested paired percentage-point differences (Δ=Counterfactual%−Generic%\Delta=\text{Counterfactual}\%-\text{Generic}\%) using two-sided exact McNemar’s tests on discordant pairs. In the full-cohort automated evaluation, paired continuous rubric contrasts were summarized by the mean within-participant difference with a 10,00010{,}000-sample percentile bootstrap 95%95\% confidence interval, a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test (with Holm–Bonferroni correction across rubric families), and three paired effect sizes (Cohen’s dzd_{z}, matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation, and Cliff’s δ\delta). Binary preference rates were summarized with Wilson 95%95\% confidence intervals, and paired safety flag rates were compared using McNemar’s test. Autorater self-consistency across repeated passes was quantified using Fleiss’ κ\kappa and Krippendorff’s α\alpha, and cross-model inter-judge agreement (gemini-3.5-flash versus gemini-3.1-pro-preview) was assessed via intra-class correlation ICC⁡(2,1)\mathrm{ICC}(2,1), Spearman’s ρ\rho, quadratic-weighted κ\kappa, and Cohen’s κ\kappa on binary preferences. Statistical significance was denoted as ∗P<0.05{}^{*}P<0.05, P∗⁣∗<0.01{}^{**}P<0.01, and ∗∗∗P<0.001{}^{***}P<0.001.

Data availability

All of Us data are accessible to registered researchers through the All of Us Researcher Workbench (https://www.researchallofus.org/). The WEAR-ME dataset is available to approved researchers for reproducibility purposes (access instructions at https://github.com/Google-Health/consumer-health-research/tree/main/insulin_resistance_prediction). De-identified longitudinal Fitbit records cannot be publicly shared due to participant consent and privacy restrictions.

Code availability

Code for Coachable Health Age, SensorWM, and all statistical analyses will be released upon publication at https://github.com/Google-Health/consumer-health-research.
