A.1 Coachable Health Age

LLM Health Age & Consistency

Within-Temperature Consistency The stochastic stability of the LLM’s estimations was evaluated by comparing the consistency of health age predictions across three runs (k=3k=3) under different temperatures (T∈{0.1,0.5,1.0}T\in\{0.1,0.5,1.0\}) for two data input configurations: (1) Raw Signals (incorporating all raw wearable sensor streams) and (2) Identical metrics that coachable Health Age algorithm receives as input. In order to be able to compare across temperatures, in cases where LLM provided a range as health age (e.g., 45-48 years), the average of the interval was used in the analysis. For the Raw Signals configuration, the model exhibited greater stability across temperatures (Supplementary Table 3). At T=0.1T=0.1, the average standard deviation (SD) between runs was low (1.351.35 years). Single-run consistency, measured by ICC(3,1), was moderate (0.540.54), and averaging across the three runs improved consistency to ICC​(3,3)=0.78\text{ICC}(3,3)=0.78. As temperature increased, consistency declined gradually: at T=0.5T=0.5, average SD rose to 2.062.06 years (ICC​(3,1)=0.30\text{ICC}(3,1)=0.30, ICC​(3,3)=0.57\text{ICC}(3,3)=0.57), and at T=1.0T=1.0, SD reached 3.373.37 years while retaining higher reliability than the curated baseline (ICC​(3,1)=0.20\text{ICC}(3,1)=0.20, ICC​(3,3)=0.42\text{ICC}(3,3)=0.42).

The Identical CHA configuration showed a sharp drop in consistency as temperature increased (Supplementary Table 3). While reliability at T=0.1T=0.1 matched the all-signals configuration in ICC (ICC​(3,1)=0.54\text{ICC}(3,1)=0.54, ICC​(3,k)=0.78\text{ICC}(3,k)=0.78) albeit with higher run-to-run spread (SD = 2.722.72 years), reliability collapsed at T=0.5T=0.5 (SD = 3.543.54 years), with single-run consistency dropping to ICC​(3,1)=0.09\text{ICC}(3,1)=0.09 and three-run average consistency only reaching ICC​(3,k)=0.23\text{ICC}(3,k)=0.23. A similar collapse was observed at T=1.0T=1.0 (SD = 3.203.20 years, ICC​(3,1)=0.11\text{ICC}(3,1)=0.11, ICC​(3,k)=0.28\text{ICC}(3,k)=0.28).

Across-Temperature Sensitivity For the Raw Signals configuration, the Friedman test indicated a statistically significant overall difference in health age estimations across the three temperatures (χ2​(2)=6.47,p=0.039\chi^{2}(2)=6.47,p=0.039). However, post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction did not detect any statistically significant differences between specific temperature pairs (T0.1T_{0.1} vs. T0.5T_{0.5}: adj. p=0.075p=0.075; T0.5T_{0.5} vs. T1.0T_{1.0}: adj. p=0.0689p=0.0689; T0.1T_{0.1} vs. T1.0T_{1.0}: adj. p=1.00p=1.00).

For the Curated Metrics configuration, the sensitivity to temperature was highly pronounced. The Friedman test revealed an extremely significant difference across temperatures (χ2​(2)=39.71,p=2.39×10−9\chi^{2}(2)=39.71,p=2.39\times 10^{-9}). Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction confirmed that estimated health ages systematically shifted across all temperature pairs (T0.1T_{0.1} vs. T0.5T_{0.5}: adj. p=0.0039p=0.0039; T0.5T_{0.5} vs. T1.0T_{1.0}: adj. p=0.0024p=0.0024; T0.1T_{0.1} vs. T1.0T_{1.0}: adj. p=7.71×10−10p=7.71\times 10^{-10}; Supplementary Table 4).

Association with standard Metrics (Modified LE8 and MSSS): To evaluate the clinical alignment of the generated health ages, we calculated the Pearson correlation coefficient (rr) between the delta health age (estimated health age minus actual age) and two established health indicators: the modified Life’s Essential 8 (mod-LE8) score and the Metabolic Syndrome Severity (MSSS) score. Across both data configurations, delta health age correlated negatively with the modified LE8 score and positively with the MSSS score (Supplementary Table 5).

Coachable Health Age Correlates with AHA Life’s Essentials 8 & Metabolic Syndrome Score

We further evaluated the clinical alignment of Coachable Health Age by examining its associations with established measures of cardiovascular and metabolic health. The American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 (LE8) framework [1] provides a comprehensive assessment of cardiovascular health across eight domains, including diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, sleep health, body mass index, blood lipids, blood glucose, and blood pressure. We considered a modified LE8 score (mod-LE8) excluding diet, alongside the Metabolic Syndrome Severity Score (MSSS) [77], a continuous measure of metabolic dysfunction incorporating BMI, blood pressure, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, and fasting glucose. CHA demonstrated the strongest absolute correlations with both mod-LE8 (|r|=0.512|r|=0.512) and MSSS (|r|=0.355|r|=0.355), outperforming chronological age and alternative biological age estimates. These findings suggest that CHA captures clinically meaningful variation in cardiometabolic health beyond that reflected by conventional age measures.

We additionally examined the relationship between wearable-derived Delta Health Age and self-reported overall health status. Consistent with the expected relationship between perceived health and physiological aging, Delta Health Age increased monotonically with worsening self-reported health, from approximately zero years among individuals reporting excellent health to over 11 years among those reporting poor health. This graded association provides complementary evidence of construct validity, suggesting that wearable-derived health age estimates reflect meaningful differences in overall health status that are consistent with individuals’ subjective assessments of their health.

A.2 Trajectory Prediction with Sensor World Model

Choosing the SensorWM

We compared two world model training formulations, Trajectory Transformer [78], which autoregressively predicts future wearable representations using a transformer backbone [79], and LeWorldModel [40], which learns action-conditioned latent dynamics through joint-embedding prediction. To determine which formulation better preserved clinically relevant information, we evaluated downstream classification performance using generated trajectories from both models against observed Fitbit data. LeWorldModel outperformed Trajectory Transformer on nine of 12 tasks, with notable improvements in insulin resistance (AUROC 0.760 vs. 0.719), smoking status (0.774 vs. 0.698), and hyperlipidemia (0.692 vs. 0.645). Based on its stronger preservation of clinically informative representations, we adopted the LeWorldModel-inspired training formulation for SensorWM (Supplementary Table 13).

Scaling SensorWM

We investigated the effect of pre-training data scale on SensorWM’s ability to generate clinically informative physiological trajectories, comparing models trained on 1k, 10k, and 100k participants. We evaluated representation quality indirectly through downstream classification performance using model-generated trajectories. As shown in Supplementary Table 14, increasing pre-training data generally improved downstream discrimination, with the 100k model achieving the highest AUROC on 8 of 12 tasks, including insulin resistance (0.760), respiratory conditions (0.660), and smoking status (0.774). Although improvements were not strictly monotonic across all tasks, these results suggest that scaling pre-training data enhances the preservation of clinically relevant information in generated physiological trajectories, motivating our use of the 100k-participant model for SensorWM.

Trajectory versus Static Classification

While world models are trained to forecast future physiological states rather than optimize directly for discriminative downstream classification, an important question is whether the longitudinal dynamics captured by the model encode information that is absent from static snapshots of wearable data. To investigate this, we compare downstream prediction performance using four different feature sources: (1) the true observed longitudinal Fitbit trajectories, (2) trajectories generated by the sensor world model, (3) representations obtained from the state of the art SensorFM [20], and (4) features derived solely from the first week of wearable observations.

This comparison isolates the value of longitudinal physiological information. Both the SensorFM and first-week baselines operate on a limited temporal view of an individual’s health state and therefore primarily capture cross-sectional physiological characteristics at a single point in time. In contrast, the observed Fitbit trajectories and the world-model-generated trajectories incorporate patterns that emerge over extended periods, including behavioral consistency, physiological adaptation, recovery dynamics, and temporal variability. These longitudinal signatures may encode information about an individual’s health that cannot be recovered from a single observation window alone helping motivate the need for having a world model capable of learning the physiological trajectories of human health. All models utilize the same Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) style classifier [80] to ensure fairness and Longitudinal Models (True Fitbit Sequence & Sensor World Model Fitbit Sequences) and SensorFM [20] latent space dimensions are fixed at D=128D=128 to ensure fair comparisons.

We therefore evaluate whether access to a longitudinal trajectory provides measurable benefits for downstream health prediction. If longitudinal physiological dynamics contain information beyond static physiological snapshots, models trained on observed or generated trajectories should outperform approaches that rely solely on single-time-point measurements. Furthermore, comparable performance between observed and generated trajectories would suggest that the sensor world model successfully preserves the clinically relevant information contained within real wearable trajectories while enabling future-state simulation and forecasting. This analysis therefore serves both as an assessment of the utility of longitudinal wearable signals and as a validation of the information fidelity of the learned world model representations.

Classification Subgroup Analysis

To evaluate the fidelity of the generated physiological trajectories, we perform a series of subgroup analyses constructed from our demographic labels stratifying by age, body mass index (BMI), and sex. The objective of these experiments is not to assess demographic fairness, but rather to determine whether SensorWM preserves clinically relevant physiological information across populations that exhibit substantially different baseline physiology, behavioral patterns, and disease prevalence. If the generated trajectories faithfully capture the underlying structure of the observed wearable signals, downstream predictive performance should remain similar when using world-model-generated features instead of the true wearable measurements.

For each demographic subgroup, we repeat the downstream prediction experiments using both observed Fitbit features and world-model-generated features. Performance is quantified using AUROC, and differences between the two feature sources are evaluated using DeLong’s test. By comparing prediction performance within individual demographic strata, we can directly assess whether the forecasting process preserves the predictive signal contained in the original wearable measurements. Large performance degradations would suggest that information relevant to a particular population is lost during forecasting, whereas comparable performance indicates that the generated trajectories maintain the physiological characteristics necessary for downstream inference.

This stratified evaluation provides a particularly stringent assessment of feature fidelity because the world model must accurately reproduce physiological dynamics across populations with distinct health profiles and behavioral patterns. Consistent agreement between models trained on observed and generated features would indicate that the learned latent dynamics capture physiologically meaningful structure and that forecasted trajectories retain much of the information present in the original wearable observations. Such preservation is essential if generated physiological states are to serve as effective surrogates for future wearable measurements in downstream health applications.

Sensitivity Analysis of Error Propagation

A fundamental challenge in world model development is understanding how forecasting errors propagate into downstream clinical predictions. Although trajectory forecasting models are typically optimized using reconstruction objectives, improvements in reconstruction accuracy do not necessarily translate into improvements in clinically relevant decision-making. We therefore performed a sensitivity analysis to quantify the relationship between trajectory forecasting error and downstream prediction consistency across all evaluation tasks.

For each participant, we first generated a future wearable trajectory using the sensor world model and computed the trajectory reconstruction error relative to the observed wearable measurements. We then applied identical downstream classifiers to both the observed and world-model-generated trajectories and calculated the absolute difference in predicted probabilities between the two predictions. This analysis provides a direct measure of error propagation, allowing us to assess whether inaccuracies in trajectory forecasting lead to meaningful changes in downstream clinical inference. Participants were further categorized according to whether the classifier predictions obtained from observed and generated trajectories were concordant or discordant.

Across nearly all prediction tasks, we observed that downstream prediction differences remained small even when trajectory reconstruction errors varied substantially (Supplementary Figure 5). Most participants clustered near the origin of the plots, indicating that generated trajectories frequently produced predictions that closely matched those obtained from the true wearable measurements. Notably, many individuals with moderate forecasting errors still exhibited highly consistent downstream predictions, suggesting that reconstruction accuracy alone is not the primary determinant of downstream utility. Instead, the world model appears to preserve the physiologically relevant structure necessary for clinical prediction despite imperfect reconstruction of individual measurements.

Discordant predictions were relatively uncommon and were concentrated among participants exhibiting larger differences in predicted probabilities. Importantly, these identified discordance pairs were not always associated with the largest trajectory reconstruction errors. In several tasks, participants with comparatively low reconstruction error nonetheless crossed classification decision boundaries, whereas others with substantially larger forecasting errors remained correctly classified. This observation suggests that downstream sensitivity depends not only on the magnitude of forecasting error but also on where that error occurs within the physiological state space. Errors affecting features strongly associated with a particular outcome may have a disproportionately large effect on prediction, whereas reconstruction errors in less informative regions may have minimal clinical consequence.

These findings indicate that the relationship between forecasting accuracy and downstream performance is highly nonlinear. While trajectory reconstruction error provides a useful measure of forecasting quality, it does not fully characterize the utility of generated physiological trajectories for clinical prediction. From a health modeling perspective, preserving the latent physiological signals relevant to downstream outcomes may be more important than perfectly reconstructing every observed wearable measurement. The overall concentration of points near low probability differences across tasks therefore provides evidence that the sensor world model retains much of the clinically meaningful information present in real wearable trajectories, even when forecasting errors accumulate over extended prediction horizons.

Feature Fidelity: Correlations

A central question is whether generated trajectories preserve the physiological relationships present in real-world sensor data. While trajectory reconstruction metrics evaluate the accuracy of individual feature forecasts, they do not assess whether the model maintains the higher-order dependencies that govern interactions between wearable features. Preserving these dependencies is essential if generated trajectories are to serve as realistic surrogates for future wearable observations. We therefore evaluated feature fidelity by comparing the correlation structure of observed and world-model-generated wearable trajectories.

For each cohort, we computed pairwise correlation matrices across all physiological and behavioral features using both the observed Fitbit trajectories and the corresponding trajectories generated by the Sensor World Model. Correlations were calculated at the population level as well as within behaviorally distinct subgroups consisting of sedentary and highly active participants. To quantify deviations from the true physiological structure, we additionally computed difference matrices representing the change in pairwise correlations between observed and generated trajectories. This analysis evaluates whether the world model preserves the statistical organization of the wearable feature space rather than simply reproducing individual measurements.

Across all cohorts, the generated trajectories closely reproduced the correlation structure observed in the original wearable data (Supplementary Figure 6, 7). Many of the strongest physiological relationships, including interactions between cardiovascular measurements, sleep architecture variables, activity metrics, and stress-related features, were preserved in the generated trajectories. The overall visual similarity between observed and generated correlation matrices suggests that the world model captures underlying physiological dependencies that extend beyond individual feature reconstruction which is a well known property of world models [34].

The difference matrices further indicate that most pairwise relationships remain stable following trajectory generation. Although localized deviations are present, particularly among a subset of activity- and sleep-related measurements, these changes are small relative to the overall correlation structure. Importantly, preservation of feature relationships was observed not only within the full population but also within sedentary and highly active cohorts, which exhibit substantially different behavioral and physiological profiles. This suggests that the world model learns physiological dynamics that generalize across heterogeneous patterns of activity rather than relying on population-average correlations alone.

These findings provide complementary evidence to the downstream prediction experiments. Whereas classification analyses evaluate whether generated trajectories preserve task-relevant predictive information, correlation analyses assess whether they preserve the broader physiological organization of the wearable feature space. The strong agreement between observed and generated correlation structures suggests that the world model retains much of the higher-order information encoded within longitudinal wearable measurements. Consequently, the generated trajectories appear to preserve both local feature behavior and global physiological structure, supporting their use as realistic simulations of future health trajectories.

A.3 Expert Evaluation of Counterfactual Coaching

The main-text expert evaluation compared Counterfactual Coaching with Generic Coaching in a blinded, randomized, paired study of 49 WEAR-ME participant cases reviewed by five certified lifestyle coaches and five board-certified clinicians. Across both expert panels, the study comprised 490 paired plan evaluations. Detailed per-rater, rubric-level, cross-disciplinary, and persona-stratified results are reported below and in Supplementary Tables 25–30.

Head-to-head preference and anticipated adherence

Lifestyle coaches completed head-to-head side-by-side comparisons of Counterfactual and Generic Coaching plans for each participant. In the set displayed in Fig. 1e, 245 valid paired comparisons were available. Counterfactual Coaching was selected as the Best Overall Plan in 71.4% of evaluations (175/245; 95% CI, 65.5–76.7%), compared with 28.6% for Generic Coaching (70/245; 95% CI, 23.3–34.5%). This corresponded to a +42.9 percentage-point difference and a 2.50-fold preference ratio (two-sided exact binomial P=1.49×10−11P=1.49\times 10^{-11}).

Lifestyle coaches also selected Counterfactual Coaching as having the Highest Likelihood of Long-Term Adherence in 71.0% of displayed evaluations (174/245; 95% CI, 65.0–76.3%), compared with 29.0% for Generic Coaching (71/245; P=3.72×10−11P=3.72\times 10^{-11}).

Preference was directionally consistent across all five lifestyle coaches. Individual-rater Counterfactual win rates ranged from 53.1% to 98.0% for Best Overall Plan and from 44.9% to 98.0% for anticipated long-term adherence (Supplementary Table 30). When evaluations were aggregated by participant using majority consensus of at least three of five coaches, Counterfactual Coaching was preferred in 43 of 49 cases (87.8%; P=5.73×10−8P=5.73\times 10^{-8}) for Best Overall Plan and in 44 of 49 cases (89.8%; P=7.60×10−9P=7.60\times 10^{-9}) for Highest Likelihood of Long-Term Adherence.

Clinical safety and physiological accuracy

Clinical safety was independently assessed by five board-certified clinicians across 245 paired evaluations. Counterfactual plans passed the Safe Intensity Limits criterion in 99.2% of evaluations (243/245; 95% CI, 97.1–99.8%), compared with 97.6% of Generic plans (239/245; 95% CI, 94.8–98.9%). The difference was not statistically significant (Δ=+1.6\Delta=+1.6 percentage points; exact McNemar P=0.289P=0.289; Supplementary Table 27).

Physiological claims were judged correct in 97.1% of Counterfactual plans (238/245) and 97.6% of Generic plans (239/245; P=1.00P=1.00). Clinicians also rated Trajectory Control highly in both conditions (96.7% [237/245] for Counterfactual and 93.1% [228/245] for Generic; Δ=+3.7\Delta=+3.7 percentage points; P=0.093P=0.093). These results indicate that the additional projected physiological information in the Counterfactual condition did not produce a detectable reduction in safety or physiological correctness.

Lifestyle coach rubric performance

We analyzed paired top-box achievement across 10 lifestyle-coach evaluation dimensions (Supplementary Table 26). Counterfactual Coaching achieved statistically significant improvements across seven of the ten dimensions.

The largest difference occurred for Contrasts Benefits vs. Status Quo. Coaches rated 73.5% of Counterfactual plans (180/245) as effectively contrasting the projected benefits of behavioral change with maintaining current behavior, compared with 5.7% of Generic plans (14/245). This corresponded to a +67.8 percentage-point difference, with 170 discordant pairs favoring Counterfactual and 4 favoring Generic (exact McNemar P=3.15×10−45P=3.15\times 10^{-45}).

Counterfactual Coaching also increased the proportion of plans judged to provide a Compelling Reason to Change without fear- or shame-based framing from 28.6% (70/245) to 75.5% (185/245), a +46.9 percentage-point difference (121 versus 6 discordant pairs; P=6.39×10−29P=6.39\times 10^{-29}). Trajectory Control similarly increased from 59.4% (145/244) for Generic Coaching to 97.1% (238/245) for Counterfactual Coaching, with 97 versus 5 discordant pairs (P=3.46×10−23P=3.46\times 10^{-23}).

On the ordinal behavior-change rubrics, Counterfactual Coaching more than doubled the frequency of Strongly Applied Behavior-Change Strategies, from 20.4% (50/245) to 50.2% (123/245; Δ=+29.8\Delta=+29.8 percentage points; 89 versus 16 discordant pairs; P=1.87×10−13P=1.87\times 10^{-13}). Excellent Sustainable Habit Building increased from 28.6% (70/245) to 52.2% (128/245; Δ=+23.7\Delta=+23.7 percentage points; 75 versus 17 discordant pairs; P=7.29×10−10P=7.29\times 10^{-10}). At the opposite end of the ordinal scales, “Absent” behavior-change strategies decreased from 4.1% (10/245) to 0.4% (1/245), while “Poor” habit building decreased from 3.3% (8/245) to 1.2% (3/245).

Counterfactual Coaching was also more frequently judged Realistic and Non-Overwhelming, with top-box ratings increasing from 82.9% (203/245) to 98.8% (242/245; Δ=+15.9\Delta=+15.9 percentage points; 41 versus 2 discordant pairs; P=2.15×10−10P=2.15\times 10^{-10}). Supportive and Motivating Tone increased from 83.3% (204/245) to 98.4% (241/245; Δ=+15.1\Delta=+15.1 percentage points; 41 versus 4 discordant pairs; P=9.33×10−9P=9.33\times 10^{-9}).

Not all dimensions differed. Top-box Signal Synthesis ratings were nearly identical between Counterfactual and Generic Coaching (49.0% [120/245] versus 48.6% [119/245]; P=1.00P=1.00). However, examination of the full ordinal distribution showed that fragmented metric reporting decreased from 19.6% (48/245) in Generic Coaching to 7.8% (19/245) in Counterfactual Coaching, with a corresponding increase in cohesive descriptive summaries (43.3% versus 29.8%).

Lifestyle-coach ratings of Baseline and Wearable Personalization showed a smaller top-box difference. In the evaluations, 54.3% of Counterfactual plans (133/245) and 51.8% of Generic plans (127/245) were rated Highly Tailored (P=0.572P=0.572). Despite similar top-box rates, bottom-box “Generic” ratings decreased from 4.1% (10/245) for Generic Coaching to 2.4% (6/245) for Counterfactual Coaching.

Easy to Understand was the only dimension with a numerically higher top-box rate for Generic Coaching: 89.8% (220/245) compared with 84.9% (208/245) for Counterfactual Coaching. The difference was not statistically significant (Δ=−4.9\Delta=-4.9 percentage points; 18 versus 30 discordant pairs; P=0.111P=0.111), but is consistent with a potential trade-off between the simplicity of a single recommendation pathway and the greater numerical density introduced by multiple projected options.

Clinician rubric performance

Clinician evaluations are summarized in Supplementary Table 27. The largest difference was again observed for Contrasts Benefits vs. Status Quo. Counterfactual Coaching achieved the top rating in 92.2% of clinician evaluations (226/245), compared with 7.8% for Generic Coaching (19/245). This represented a +84.5 percentage-point difference, with 213 discordant pairs favoring Counterfactual and 6 favoring Generic (P=3.49×10−55P=3.49\times 10^{-55}).

Clinicians also rated Counterfactual plans as Highly Tailored to the participant’s physiological profile more often than Generic plans (72.2% [177/245] versus 52.2% [128/245]; Δ=+20.0\Delta=+20.0 percentage points; 82 versus 33 discordant pairs; P=5.57×10−6P=5.57\times 10^{-6}).

Twelve-week Biological Plausibility was rated positively in 86.1% of Counterfactual plans (211/245) compared with 81.6% of Generic plans (200/245), corresponding to a +4.5 percentage-point difference (18 versus 7 discordant pairs; P=0.043P=0.043). The smaller magnitude of this effect relative to the trajectory-framing and personalization measures indicates that the primary clinician-perceived contribution of the counterfactual system was not a generalized increase across all clinical dimensions, but improved linkage between participant-specific physiology, candidate actions, and projected outcomes.

Cross-disciplinary concordance and divergence

Three evaluation dimensions were shared between lifestyle coaches and clinicians, allowing comparison of how the two expert groups interpreted the same plans.

Both groups strongly favored Counterfactual Coaching for Contrasts Benefits vs. Status Quo, with a pooled difference of +76.1 percentage points (P<10−98P<10^{-98}). This was the most consistent cross-disciplinary signal and directly reflected the additional future-versus-future information available to the Counterfactual coach.

The groups differed more substantially in their interpretation of Trajectory Control. Clinicians rated both Generic and Counterfactual plans highly on this dimension (93.1% and 96.7%, respectively), reflecting that both conditions provided safe, modifiable, phased recommendations. Lifestyle coaches applied a stricter behavioral interpretation: Generic plans received a top-box rating in 59.4% of evaluations compared with 97.1% for Counterfactual plans. Coach feedback indicated that the explicit presentation of multiple behavioral options in Counterfactual plans increased perceived autonomy and choice relative to a single prescribed pathway.

The opposite pattern was observed for Baseline and Wearable Personalization. Clinicians gave Counterfactual Coaching a +20.0 percentage-point top-box advantage (72.2% versus 52.2%; P<0.001P<0.001), whereas lifestyle-coach ratings were more similar (54.3% versus 51.8%; P=0.572P=0.572). Clinicians appeared to place greater weight on quantitative alignment between the plan and physiological drivers such as Health Age and resting heart rate. Lifestyle coaches noted in free-text responses that physiological tailoring alone did not capture important psychosocial constraints, including work schedules, caregiving responsibilities, and access to exercise resources.

Performance across WEAR-ME Coachable Personas

To evaluate whether the observed preference was restricted to a particular participant phenotype, we stratified results across five prespecified WEAR-ME Coachable Personas (Fig. 5c; Supplementary Table 29).

Among Multi-Risk Challenger participants characterized by low activity, insufficient sleep, elevated BMI, and accelerated Health Age, Counterfactual Coaching achieved its highest side-by-side preference. It was selected as the Best Overall Plan in 80.0% of comparisons (40/50; P=2.39×10−5P=2.39\times 10^{-5}) and as having the highest likelihood of long-term adherence in 82.0% (41/50; P=5.61×10−6P=5.61\times 10^{-6}). The largest rubric differences included Trajectory Control (+48.0 percentage points; 100% versus 52%), Behavior-Change Strategies (+32.0 points; 48% versus 16%), Sustainable Habits (+26.0 points; 50% versus 24%), and Realistic and Manageable Routine Fit (+26.0 points; 100% versus 74%). Counterfactual plans more often presented distinct behavioral entry points rather than requiring simultaneous changes across multiple domains.

This subgroup also revealed a calibration limitation. Clinicians rated 12-week Biological Plausibility slightly lower for Counterfactual than Generic plans (76% versus 82%; Δ=−6.0\Delta=-6.0 percentage points). Free-text comments indicated that model-projected Health Age reductions of approximately 4–5 years following modest 12-week changes in activity or sleep appeared overly optimistic in some participant cases.

Among Activity Bottleneck participants with isolated inactivity and preserved sleep, Counterfactual Coaching was preferred in 74.0% of comparisons (37/50; P=0.0009P=0.0009). This subgroup showed the largest persona-specific gains in coach-rated Trajectory Control (+54.0 percentage points; 100% versus 46%) and Behavior-Change Strategies (+34.0 points; 44% versus 10%), as well as a +38.0 percentage-point gain in clinician-rated Baseline Personalization (76% versus 38%). Clinician feedback highlighted that Counterfactual plans more often preserved already-adequate sleep and concentrated recommendations on progressive activity increases.

Among Optimal Baseline participants with high activity, adequate sleep, and a relatively younger Health Age, Counterfactual Coaching was selected as the Best Overall Plan in 72.0% of comparisons (36/50; P=0.0026P=0.0026) and as having the highest likelihood of long-term adherence in 70.0% (35/50; P=0.0066P=0.0066). Counterfactual plans showed higher ratings for Trajectory Control (+34.7 percentage points; 100% versus 65%), Sustainable Habits (+28.0 points; 64% versus 36%), and clinician-rated 12-week Biological Plausibility (+18.0 points; 98% versus 80%). Coaches noted that Generic plans more often prescribed unnecessary increases in activity volume despite already-high baseline activity, whereas Counterfactual plans more often emphasized maintenance and recovery.

Among Balanced Maintainer participants with population-median behavioral profiles, Counterfactual Coaching was selected in 71.1% of comparisons (32/45; P=0.0066P=0.0066) for both Best Overall Plan and anticipated long-term adherence. This subgroup showed the largest persona-specific improvement in Behavior-Change Strategies (+42.2 percentage points; 58% versus 16%) and a +26.7 percentage-point increase in clinician-rated Baseline Personalization (78% versus 51%).

The smallest preference margin occurred among Recovery Bottleneck participants characterized by high activity and insufficient sleep. Counterfactual Coaching was preferred in 60.0% of valid displayed comparisons (30/50) compared with 40.0% for Generic Coaching. Clinicians nevertheless rated Counterfactual plans as more physiologically personalized by +18.0 percentage points (70% versus 52%), in part because the plans more often identified sleep extension as the principal modifiable pathway for already-active participants.

Lifestyle coaches were less favorable in this subgroup, with Baseline and Wearable Personalization ratings 14.0 percentage points lower for Counterfactual Coaching (44% versus 58%). Free-text feedback suggested that some Counterfactual plans continued to include additional step increases for participants already averaging approximately 10,000–14,000 steps per day because their historical peaks exceeded 16,000 steps per day. Coaches viewed these additional activity options as diluting the more appropriate recovery-focused recommendation.

Together, the persona-stratified analyses indicate that the preference for Counterfactual Coaching was not confined to participants with a single behavioral deficit or elevated Health Age. The analysis also identified two recurrent limitations: redundant recommendations in behavioral domains that were already near saturation, and potentially over-optimistic short-horizon Health Age projections in some high-risk participants.
